speakeroldname: Righi Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minisfer):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: STATEMENT ON FURTHER LEGISLATIVE PROGRAM FOR SESSION
speechtext:
There are several matters to which I wish to refer. The first is this. I undertook to place before the house the general plan of the legislation to be introduced before this session ends.
The house, of course, is fully aware of the various items set forth in the speech from the throne on January 14, 1960. Generally speaking I think all the items referred to therein will have received the attention of the house before the session concludes, with one exception; that is the undertaking to bring in amendments to the Expropriation
Act. The house will recall that an action was tried before Mr. Justice Thorson regarding the general field of expropriation, and that judgment laid open to perilous possibilities the expropriation proceedings which had been taken throughout the years. However, the Supreme Court of Canada reversed the judgment of Mr. Justice Thorson; therefore there is no immediate need at this session to proceed with the amendments to the Expropriation Act.
Now with respect to the matters yet to be dealt with; No. 1-and in numbering them in this way I do not, of course, undertake that they will be brought forward in this order- the bill of rights; No. 2, the act to set up the department of forestry; No. 3, the amendments to the Canada Elections Act; No. 4, the amendment to the Freight Rates Reduction Act made necessary by the probability that the royal commission on transportation will not have been able to report prior to the expiry date of the legislation now in effect, that date being July 31; No. 5, the Civil Service Act; No. 6, the Civil Service Superannuation Act.
In addition to these there are a number of matters of legislation now before the other place which will have to be dealt with here as well. There is the trade treaty with Russia; amendments to the Canada Shipping Act; amendments to the Criminal Code, and a bill respecting the international boundary. As I say, the four last named are now before the other place.
In general I think that covers the various matters which will be brought before the house this session in addition, of course, to such matters as are already on the order paper.
There is another matter on which the house desires information, and that has to do with the private bill on capital punishment introduced by the hon. member for York-Scar-borough (Mr. McGee). I am not going into the details of the discussion with regard thereto. I will, however, refer to one or two references in Hansard. On March 11, as reported on page 2012, a question was asked about what was going to be done in this connection. At that time the house leader said:
The matter is under consideration, but I know the house is anxious to press on with some of the legislation that is on the order paper.
He added:
This will not prevent subsequent consideration of the debate on capital punishment at a later date.

Business of the House
Then on March 21 the hon. member for Laurier asked me when the government intended to make arrangements for the resumption of the debate on the private bill concerning capital punishment now before the house. There was some discussion regarding certain statements made outside the house by hon. members, and my reply that day, as will be found on page 2252, was:
At the present time the order paper contains a number of matters which require attention. When these matters have received consideration then, as the result of consultation among the house leader, the hon. gentleman and a representative of the C.C.F., a determination in this regard can be made.
While there were other references made on other occasions, I feel that those to which I have referred are sufficient to indicate a summary of the situation.
The interpretation given to the words I used in the house in connection with this matter was that a further day would be allowed or provided for. That being so, while there is much yet to be done, I feel the proper course to follow would be this. Consultation having taken place among the leader of the house, the hon. member for Laurier and the hon. member for Assiniboia, if a motion made later on in the session to provide a private members' day were accepted by the house, then an opportunity would be provided to deal with this and other matters that are appropriate to a private members' day. In other words, the undertaking given is being carried out. The house will have an opportunity on a private members' day later in the session, when we have removed from the order paper many of the things which require to be done, to discuss the bill of the hon. member for York-Scarborough.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: STATEMENT ON FURTHER LEGISLATIVE PROGRAM FOR SESSION
speechtext:
We have reached June 14, and we began on January 14. The house has been in session now for five months and we have, on this five months' anniversary, received from the Prime Minister an indication of the work that remains to be done, including some important pieces of legislation which are not yet on the order paper. That is its own commentary on the manner in which the business of this house has been conducted.
May I mention first what the Prime Minister dealt with last. With regard to the private member's bill on capital punishment, the Prime Minister has indicated-and I have no quarrel whatever with the suggestion -that, if it is desired, a private members' day may be set aside on which this matter which has aroused so much interest in the country can be further discussed. I think
[Mr. DiefenbakerJ
the expression used by the Prime Minister was so that it could, if possible, be dealt with.
I do not know whether the Prime Minister had in mind using the expression "dealt with" coming to a decision by a vote of the house on this matter. If so, I am sure the Prime Minister will agree, as he has already indicated, that that decision can only be reached-in my view at least-if all those hon. members who wish to speak on this matter have had the same opportunity to do so as has been given to those who have already spoken. Perhaps, therefore, it will not be possible in a day to come to a decision on this matter, and possibly during the recess-if we do not run into the next session of parliament-the government may desire to give consideration to what action, if any, the government itself should take in a subsequent session.
So far as the business of the house is concerned, the Prime Minister has pointed out that there are seven or eight important pieces of legislation yet to be introduced, including a bill of rights. There are also, as I calculate, ten or eleven pieces of legislation in various stages of progress in the house at the present time. If these matters are to be given the consideration they deserve-and so far as we on this side of the house are concerned we will do our best to see that they get that kind of consideration-it is obvious that a good many weeks will be required before they can be dealt with. I am not complaining about that, but I think we should be quite aware of the situation. Consideration of all these items, some of which will require careful and long consideration, will surely mean that we cannot possibly finish the business of this house before the end of July.
Quite apart from the legislation, the list of which I have before me, including two or three new items the Prime Minister mentioned this morning, we have various committees sitting. Indeed, seven committees are meeting today and I believe ten committees met yesterday. This afternoon when we will presumably be discussing one of the most important subjects any Canadian parliament could discuss, the amendment of our constitution, there will be three committees meeting which will make it impossible for some hon. members to participate in that discussion. There is one important committee that has not yet even been set up, the committee on broadcasting. The committee considering the Civil Service Act amendments will require time to give these matters the consideration to which they are entitled. It is obvious that the work of this committee will take some time. There will be witnesses to be heard in the discussion of the amendments to the

combines act. I hope that even in the light of the experience that has already taken place the defence expenditures committee will hear witnesses on that subject.
So far as the estimates are concerned we have finished one department, agriculture, except for the supplementaries. That is the only department of government the estimates of which have been concluded at the present time. I mention this so that no one will be in any doubt as to the amount of time that will be required this session to give the business of government the consideration to which it is entitled, and to carry on that business in a careful, methodical and efficient way.
In those circumstances we can look forward, I believe, to a very active and I hope constructive summer.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: STATEMENT ON FURTHER LEGISLATIVE PROGRAM FOR SESSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister outlined a very elaborate program that must be dealt with before the conclusion of this session. It has always seemed to me that it would help expedite the procedure during any session if we could have this kind of tabulation at the beginning so we would know at an early date the things that we would necessarily be dealing with during the session. As to a number of items, we have been uncertain whether the government was going to proceed with them or whether they would be dropped.
The Prime Minister has said that he is quite agreeable to having the debate on capital punishment come forward for a further day of debate. We in the C.C.F. would like to see this bill come to a vote, and we are quite prepared to give consideration at any time to a motion to provide for an additional day's debate on the bill to abolish capital punishment in the hope that a vote could be reached, and that the result of the vote would be to have the bill passed at this session.
I think the duty of the members of the House of Commons is to deal efficiently and carefully with the business as presented to the house. It is obvious from the list that has been given this morning and from the statement of the Leader of the Opposition that if there is no adjournment of this session, to be resumed at a later date, we shall be here for the summer. Now, a summer in Ottawa dealing with parliamentary duties puts many members of the House of Commons at a very great disadvantage. Many members have their families a long way from Ottawa; children are out of school during July and August, and this is the time when hon. members like to be with their families. Therefore it is a great sacrifice that members must make if the session continues.
79951-0-308
Business of the House
Those of us who have had the experience of sitting in Ottawa during the summer months know that summer conditions in Ottawa, with the house meeting morning, afternoon and evening, to say the least are not conducive to the health of members of parliament. We feel that there is growing evidence to support the suggestion of the C.C.F. party that parliament would be enabled to deal more adequately with our legislation if we had a summer adjournment and came back later this year to conclude the remainder of the business of this session. However, with the Leader of the Opposition, we shall deal with each piece of legislation as it is presented to the house in a way that we think is in keeping with our duties.

speechtext: I agree with both hon. gentlemen that the proper responsibility of the House of Commons is to examine each piece of legislation carefully and exhaustively. All I can say in that regard is that I like parliament to be sitting, because it is very helpful to get the views of hon. members and to understand the thinking of Canadians as a whole. I think that is one of the reasons I suggested the setting up of a committee on rules, to the end that hon. members would be able, through that committee, to bring forward recommendations and suggestions which, without in any way limiting the first responsibility of the House of Commons for a careful examination, will assure efficient and effective discussion taking place without repetitious utterances which are not always synonymous with a careful examination.

Business of the House
Mention was made of the number of committees, and certainly we have a large number of committees sitting. I think it could be said for the establishment of these committees, on a more extensive scale than ever before, that they have been effective and thorough and that the members of the various committees are entitled to the commendation of the house as a whole. I know it is difficult when important matters come before the house for committee members to be always present. But I hope, as I said earlier, that when such matters of great importance are before the house the committees, as a whole, would agree to the necessary measures of adjournment to the end that those members of the committees who wish to participate in those discussions would be given the opportunity to do so.
That is all I intend to say. I feel sure that if we apply ourselves with energy, without in any way diminishing or abdicating our responsibility, we shall be able, before this session concludes as a continuous session, to have dealt with all the matters to which reference has been made.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
That a humble address be presented to Her Majesty the Queen in the following words:
To the Queen's Most Excellent Majesty:
Most Gracious Sovereign:
We, Your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal subjects, the commons of Canada in parliament assembled, humbly approach Your Majesty, praying that you may graciously be pleased to cause a measure to be laid before the parliament of the United Kingdom to be expressed as follows:
An act to amend the British North America Act, 1867.
Whereas the Senate and commons of Canada in parliament assembled have submitted addresses to Her Majesty praying that Her Majesty may graciously be pleased to cause a measure to be laid before the parliament of the United Kingdom for the enactment of the provisions hereinafter set forth:
Be it therefore enacted by the Queen's Most Excellent Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and commons, in this present parliament assembled, and by the authority of the same, as follows:
1.	Section ninety nine of the British North America Act, 1867 is hereby repealed and the following substituted therefor:
"99. (1) Subject to subsection two of this section, the judges of the superior, district and county courts shall hold office during good behaviour, but shall be removable by the Governor General on address of the Senate and House of Commons.
(2) A judge of a superior, district or county court, whether appointed before or after the coming into force of this section, shall cease to hold office upon attaining the age of seventy five years, or upon the coming into force of this section if at that time he has already attained that age."
2.	This act may be cited as the British North America Act, 1960, and the British North America Act, 1867 to 1952, and this act may be cited together as the British North America Acts, 1867 to 1960.
3.	This act shall come into force on the first day of September nineteen hundred and sixty.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in rising to move that a humble address be presented to Her Majesty I wish to summarize the nature of the address and point out at once that later on during the course of this debate, which I trust will be carried on by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton), an amendment will be asked of the house in respect to the last paragraph, section 99, subsection 3, to which I will make detailed reference in a moment.
I begin by pointing out that section 99 now reads as follows:
-the judges of the superior, district and county courts shall hold office during good behaviour, but shall be removable by the Governor General on address of the Senate and House of Commons.
Amendment to B.N.A. Act
The change, of course, is in respect to those courts mentioned-superior, district and county courts-to the effect that judges of those courts shall cease to hold office upon attaining the age of 75 years or upon the coming into force of the section if at that time they have already attained that age.
I wish to point out immediately that there is nothing unusual in the course being followed in connection with this address. In 1906, in the revised statutes, legislation respecting judges of the Supreme Court of Canada provided for no retirement age. Then in 1927 an amendment was made to the Supreme Court Act and also to the Exchequer Court Act which in effect was similar to the one being requested of the house today. As hon. members know, in the original constitution of those courts there was no provision for retirement on the basis of age, and on March 25, 1927, an amendment was brought before the House of Commons which read:
Provided that each judge whether heretofore appointed or hereafter to be appointed shall cease to hold office upon attaining the age of 75 years, or immediately, if he has already attained that age.
I feel that this legislation which we now introduce is exactly on a par with the legislation which was introduced in 1927 amending the Supreme Court Act. There was some discussion in the House of Commons at that time regarding the applicability of the legislation to existent judges, but it was answered by the then minister of justice. When the legislation found its way to the other place there was no discussion there of any consequence. The motion in the Senate was moved by Right Hon. Raoul Dandurand. There was some question raised by one of the opposition senators to the effect that the legislation applied to existent judges. He said he himself took no objection whatever, but there were one or two of his colleagues who would like to discuss the matter. However, they never did discuss it, and two days later the legislation was passed and came into effect bringing about a change respecting the two highest courts in the country which is now asked for in so far as the courts covered by this address are concerned.
I realize that it is always a matter of interest that we in Canada, an independent country within the commonwealth, have not yet secured the right to amend our own constitution. Endeavours have been made throughout the years; the subject has been discussed over and over again. To me it is a political paradox and inconsistent with Canada's status that Canada should be required to secure its amendments to the constitution, other than those amendments which come within the exclusive authority and jurisdiction of the federal parliament, by an

Amendment to B.N.A. Act
address being taken to the mother of parliaments at Westminster. But we have no other course open to us, for up to the present time it has been found difficult if not impossible to secure agreement with the provinces as to the means whereby the authority to amend Canada's constitution shall be vested in the parliament of Canada with the approval or co-operation of the provinces as determined by agreement.
For that reason-and it is not because the United Kingdom parliament is anxious to retain its power or its authority-the change has not been made. I reiterate, it is because Canadians have been unable to agree on a method of amendment that would be generally acceptable. Indeed, in so far as the other countries of the commonwealth are concerned-the British commonwealth or the old commonwealth, whichever term you choose to use-Canada is the only country which has no provision made for the amendment of its own constitution.
To date there have been 17 occasions since 1867 when amendments to the British North America Act have been made. The question as to whether the consent of the provinces is or is not requisite does not have any application to the present motion, for all the provinces have agreed on the amendment. Indeed, each and every one of them has given complete support to the provision that the judges of these courts-the judges of the superior, district and county courts-should retire at the age of 75 years. Incidentally, all parts of the world which recognize the parliamentary and judical system have accepted this age as an appropriate one at which judges should retire.
I have mentioned the various occasions upon which this procedure has been used, and I think it would be of interest that I should refer to them in general. Each and all of the amendments to date have been as the result of an address or resolution, either joint or individual, passed by both houses, except in 1878, at which time an amendment was made providing for parliament's right to pass laws to examine witnesses and in 1895 when an amendment was passed to provide for the removal of doubts as to the right of parliament to set up the office of deputy speaker.
In so far as the amendment itself is concerned, I have already mentioned the fact that this is similar in nature to the one that was accepted in 1927 under the administration of Right Hon. Mackenzie King; and the fact that the suggestion of retirement at 75 has been accepted by all the attorneys general is a fairly effective answer to any criticism that might be made, representative as these provincial governments are of every variety


of Canadian political thought. Indeed, the only Liberal government is the government of Newfoundland. I am sure that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill), being a constitutional authority in his own right, will be much impressed in considering this matter and the attitude he will take on it by the fact that a letter from the attorney general of that province addressed to the Minister of Justice and incidentally concluding with the words "kindest regards"-

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: But the letter is addressed to the Minister of Justice.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
reads as follows:
The government of Newfoundland has no objection to the government of Canada requesting an amendment to the British North America Act-[DOT] providing for the compulsory retirement of judges of the superior, county and district courts in each province on reaching the age of 75 years.
The letter in question appears in Votes and Proceedings of February 16, 1960.
I mentioned a moment ago the various motions that had been made for amendments to the British North America Act through the years, and for the purpose of the record I will place on Hansard the several amendments.
1.	The amendment of 1871 was designed to remove doubts about the competence of the Canadian parliament to establish new provinces in the territories.
2.	The amendment of 1875. In 1873 the Canadian parliament passed an act providing for the examination of witnesses on oath by committees of the Senate and House of Commons and the constitutionality of such an act was in question; hence the amendment.
3.	The amendment of 1886. The purpose of this act was to empower the parliament of Canada to provide from time to time for the representation of the territories in the Senate and House of Commons.
4.	The Canada (Ontario Boundary) Act of 1889, the object of which was to determine the boundaries of the province of Ontario in certain particulars.
5.	The Canadian Speaker (Appointment of Deputy) Act of 1895 to which I have already made reference.
6.	The amendment of 1907 to the British North America Act to remedy the difficulties involved in the application of section 118 of the British North America Act, which determined the amount of federal subsidies to the provinces.
7.	The amendment of 1915, the object of which was to recast the composition of the Senate and to provide that a province should always be entitled to a minimum number of

members in the House of Commons equal to the number of senators representing that province.
8.	The amendment of 1916, the object of which was to lengthen the term of the existing parliament for one year in order to avoid an election at a critical stage of the war.
9.	The amendment of 1930 to transfer the resources of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta to those provinces.
10.	The passing of the statute of Westminster in 1931 constituted in effect an amendment to the British North America Act particularly with reference to the application of the colonial laws validity act.
11.	The amendment of 1940. By this act the authority to legislate on unemployment insurance was transferred from provincial to federal jurisdiction. This was a case in which all nine provinces assented to the proposed constitutional amendment.
12.	The amendment of 1943. The object of this act was to suspend until after the war the operation of the constitutional provisions requiring that the representation of the provinces in the House of Commons be readjusted on the basis of the census of 1941. This was a very interesting amendment in so far as the reaction of the province of Quebec was concerned. The legislative assembly of Quebec unanimously protested against the proposal and requested the federal authorities to modify their position.
13.	The amendment of 1946. The object of this act was to change the system of representation in the House of Commons. In this case there was no consultation with the provincial governments. This gave rise to some controversy. In the meantime, between 1943 and 1946, if I remember correctly, there had been a change in the administration in the province of Quebec. The provincial government again protested. The government of Mr. Mackenzie King contended that since the jurisdiction given to the federal parliament over certain matters is exclusive, no body other than parliament is competent under the constitution to decide on amending the constitutional rules which govern the exercise of that jurisdiction.
14.	The amendment of 1949. The object of this act was to bring Newfoundland into confederation. Arguments were advanced at that time. The Progressive Conservative opposition contended that the constitution should not be varied in any important way except by consultation with the provinces, but that did not command the support of parliament and the address was passed.
15.	The amending act of 1949. The object of this act was to enact a new section 91 (1)
79951-0-309
Amendment to B.N.A. Act which gives power to the federal parliament to amend the constitution of Canada except in a number of matters concerning provincial sovereignty or minority rights and also concerning certain rights of the House of Commons. At that time protests were made by the premier of Quebec and the premier of Alberta against the proposed unilateral action of the federal parliament and requesting that the government resolution be held in abeyance until a proposed constitutional conference could meet. The premier of Ontario expressed doubt, and I quote-*
-as to the advisability of dealing with the matter without first attempting general agreement.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
I mentioned what the attitude was. In any event, there was a vote in the house on the question. The amendment of the Conservative opposition at that time was that action should be deferred on the resolution until the proposed constitutional conference could deal with the whole problem of amending procedure, and that was negatived.
Then in 1951, following the federal-provincial conference held in December, 1950, it was decided to amend the British North America Act, by adding a section, 94 A, giving to the parliament of Canada the power to make laws in relation to old age pensions, provided that those laws would not affect the operation of any law, present or future, of a provincial legislature in relation to old age pensions. In this case there was unanimous consent on the part of all the provinces.

Amendment to B.N.A. Act
In 1952 there was a further amendment to provide for the readjustment of representation in the House of Commons, establishing a floor whereby the representation of any province would not fall by any more than 15 per cent in any one adjustment; subject, however, to the qualification that the rule would not work out in such a manner that the representation of a province with a smaller population would be greater than that of a province with a larger population. To that the Progressive Conservative opposition presented an amendment requesting previous consultation with the provinces with regard to the readjustment of representation, but the views of the opposition did not command the support of the house and were voted down by a vote of 121 to 27.
These are the amendments to date which have come before parliament in the 93 years since confederation. In so far as the merits of the measure are concerned, my learned and honourable colleague the Minister of Justice, will deal with those factors in detail, and also carry on the debate throughout its course.
I trust that the measure will appeal to the house. The judiciary represents the hard basis of freedom, and above everything else it must be assured that it shall operate as efficiently and effectively as it does honestly and objectively. The judiciary of Canada, of all the courts, have never been subject to challenge. Its inviolability is accepted by all. The assurance that our courts have at all times justice as their objective is recognized and accepted by all Canadians. The reason for the amendment is simply the fact that experience has shown that, while there are exceptions, when one attains the age of 75 in the judicial field it is an appropriate time and anniversary for retirement.
I mentioned, Mr. Speaker, that there was one change in the resolution that the house would be asked to accept. Clause 99 subclause 3 reads:
This act shall come into force on the first day of September nineteen hundred and sixty.
My colleague the Minister of Justice will move an amendment whenever his opportunity to speak comes, to change the date to the first day of March, 1961. The reasons which I advance in support of the change are, first, that when the resolution was placed on the order paper it was thought that it might be found possible to deal with it at an earlier time in the session, thereby making it appropriate to have the effective date September 1. This is an address to Her Majesty, praying that she will cause legislation to be enacted by the United Kingdom parliament, and it is not desirable that there be in the terms of

such an address any limitation on time which could have the appearance of putting pressure on the sovereign to whom the prayer is addressed, or to the United Kingdom parliament which will be asked to deal with it.
Second, there are a number of adjustments which will have to be made at the time the legislation becomes effective. Parliament is being asked in other legislation, notice of which has been given in a resolution now before the house, to make changes in the pension provision affecting all judges, including those whose retirement becomes automatic by virtue of their reaching, or having reached, the age of 75. It seems appropriate, especially in dealing with the judiciary, that time be given to consider the nature and effect of such changes, and without there being any appearance of undue haste.
In view, therefore, of the fact that this resolution and the concurrent legislation are not being dealt with until some months after the speech from the throne, it is hoped that the house will agree to extend the period a further six months, and the clause will then read:
This act shall come into force on the first day of March nineteen hundred and sixty one.
Sir, I think that is all I have to say with regard to this motion for an address. My hope is that it will commend itself to the house.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
I am quite happy naturally, Mr. Speaker, to fall into the normal procedure which has been mentioned by the Prime Minister. If the Minister of Justice, when he speaks, makes some of my observations unnecessary, then perhaps I shall not be accused of that repetitious irrelevancy which has been mentioned already this morning.

May I say at the very beginning that so far as the amendments to this address are concerned that have been proposed by the Prime Minister this morning, they are noncontentious, as I understand them. They are no doubt inevitable because of the delay in dealing with this matter in this House of Commons. It would not be possible, perhaps, to have all the necessary action taken here and in Westminster by the first day of September, 1960; therefore the change from that date to the first day of March, 1961, seems to me to be necessary.
Now, Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that there can be nothing much more important that can come before this house than a resolution which in effect, if it is adopted, amends our constitutional changes. This possibility could care in a matter of this kind because we are asking another parliament to take this action for us, for reasons which the Prime Minister explained this morning but which do not, as I understand the situation, cover all the provisions of this particular address.
However, I will come to that later. The necessity for special care and special consideration is made the greater because at this time, as the Prime Minister pointed out, we have at least the right, by action of the Canadian government, to amend our own constitution in respect of matters which are not exclusively within provincial jurisdiction; to that degree the amendment of our constitution has been cleared up, as the Prime Minister pointed out. There is no difficulty, of course, about matters which are exclusively provincial in character. There has been difficulty which up to the present has been insurmountable in respect of matters between those two extremes, matters which are of concern and interest and which fall in part within the jurisdiction of both federal and provincial governments.
Unfortunately over the years we have not been able to make any progress or very little progress in this field, so that the situation today is that this country of ours, which is a free and independent nation, this federal state, is still required to go to another parliament for action in respect of the amending of its own constitution in many important respects. Until we can reach agreement on this matter we will never be able to talk with the conviction with which we would like to talk about the sovereignty and independence of our country in these matters. I know that we have adopted this course by our own action, of our own free will. There is no question of any other jurisdiction imposing its will upon us.
As a matter of fact, our inability in this country to solve this constitutional problem
79951-0-3091
Amendment to B.N.A. Act is becoming more and more an embarrassment to the United Kingdom parliament itself. That parliament has already indicated in recent years that it would be very happy indeed to get rid of this responsibility, even if it is only, as I suppose it is now, a technical responsibility. The difficulty, of course, lies in the nature of our federal constitution; because I think we all agree in this house-I hope we all agree-that there can be no procedure for amending our own constitution which would be acceptable in Canada which does not preserve inviolate the rights of every province.
There can be no other solution found which would be acceptable. But sometimes we forget that the implication of this stand-and it is the only proper stand as I see it that we can take-might mean that a situation could arise where a provincial government, supported perhaps in the last election by not more than 25,000 or 30,000 Canadian elec-ors, would have a veto power over certain constitutional changes- This possibility could arise because every province would have the same right as every other province in a matter which concerned all provinces. I do not see what other principle could be adopted if the matter concerned every province. This is the price we pay for our federal system.
We have managed to work it fairly successfully up to the present, but it does, in principle at least, imply a certain rigidity which attaches, I suppose to every federal structure and which might create its own difficulties if it is not effectively managed. When I use the word "managed" I do not mean managed in a way which would interfere in any way with the rights of any particular province. The Prime Minister has made quite a point of the fact that the Minister of Justice in respect of this particular amendment, has consulted every provincial government, and that is on the record in Hansard.
Now, the care and consideration which would naturally be required in respect to any amendment to the constitution is all the greater, and I think should be all the greater, for this particular government because of words the Prime Minister used earlier in this session, when he said as recorded on page 65 of Hansard:
Here at this session of parliament, in order to secure an amendment to our constitution on a matter that is of national importance affecting the jurisdiction of both the federal and provincial parliaments and legislatures of our country, it is still necessary for us to seek an amendment from the parliament in the United Kingdom. My hope is that the time will not be too long delayed when as a result of an agreement between the federal and provincial authorities we will arrive at a point where this particular phase will be eliminated, to the end that we will be able within our own

Amendment to B.N.A. Act
country to arrive at a basis tor the amendment of our constitution agreeable to all and within the constitutional limitations ol sections 91 and 92.
I think every member of this house will echo that hope, and add the hope that progress might be made in the solution of this problem. But in view of the situation that confronts us today, and the necessity of going to another parliament for an amendment, it seems to me that unless there is urgent need for such an amendment we should not ask the parliament at Westminster to discharge what is after all, in effect if not in law, our own responsibility in Canada. Even when there is no possible doubt about the matter being one that requires a British rather than a Canadian parliamentary decision, or a British decision in addition to a Canadian parliamentary decision, we should be careful.
The first question that occurs to me with regard to this address, Mr. Speaker, is whether there is any urgency about this matter, quite apart from the question of its desirability. I suggest that the Prime Minister has not made out any case for urgency. Indeed, a look at the resolution will indicate why it would not be easy to do so. This resolution seeks the adoption of an address to be presented to Her Majesty praying that she be pleased to cause to be laid before the parliament of the United Kingdom a measure to amend the British North America Act by repealing the present section 99 and replacing it with a new section which would, if it became law, contain two paragraphs which would read as follows, and I am not quoting from the address. The new section 99(1) would read as follows:
99. (1) Subject to subsection two of this section, the judges of the superior, district and county courts shall hold office during good behaviour, but shall be removable by the Governor General on address of the Senate and House of Commons.
Subsection 2 of the new section 99 would read as follows:
(2) A judge of a superior, district or county court, whether appointed before or after the coming into force of this section, shall cease to hold office upon attaining the age of seventy five years, or upon the coming into force of this section if at that time he has already attained that age.
It is clear, then, that three changes are proposed in this resolution which, if carried and if action were taken in Great Britain, would amend our constitution. These three changes are as follows:
1.	To provide, by an amendment to the B.N.A. Act, for the compulsory retirement of judges of the superior courts at the age of 75 years.
2.	To add a provision to the British North America Act to the effect that judges of

district and county courts shall be removable only on address of the Senate and House of Commons.
3.	To fix in the constitution, by a provision in the British North America Act, the age of compulsory retirement of judges of district and county courts.
I should like to deal with each one of these changes separately. The first is the provision for the retirement of superior court judges, that is to say judges of the superior or supreme courts of the various provinces, including appeal courts. All such judges now hold office during good behaviour, that is to say, for life; and they do so, of course, because section 99 of the British North America Act, which it is now proposed to change, provides expressly as follows:
99. The judges of the superior courts shall hold office during good behaviour, but shall be removable by the Governor General on address of the Senate and House of Commons.
By this resolution the government is now proposing that all these judges of superior courts, without distinction, shall compulsorily retire at the age of 75 years. The proposed amendment does not say, as it might have said, that judges of the superior courts hereafter appointed shall cease to hold office when they attain the age of 75 years. Indeed, that was the course that was followed in the United Kingdom parliament in 1959, last year, in an amendment to the judicial pensions bill which applied only to judges hereafter appointed. That was the course that was followed in the United Kingdom.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT

speechtext: They had the option to come under it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
Yes, but it did not apply to existing judges. As I understand this British amendment-and the minister will correct me if I am wrong-it did not prejudice the financial position of any judge appointed before the act was passed. This resolution is different, however. To all the judges now in office in these courts it says, "Although you were appointed for life, and although you accepted the appointment on that understanding, the government is proposing that these conditions should be altered and therefore you will now retire when you reach 75 years of age, even though you are still capable of performing the duties of your office".
We should realize that no amendment of the British North America Act is required in order to bring about the compulsory retirement of judges who are incapable of fulfilling their duties, whether or not they have attained the age of 75 years. The Judges Act makes this fact perfectly clear in section 31, which gives to the Minister of Justice the

means of bringing about the retirement of any judge, whatever his age, who has become "incapacitated or disabled from the due execution of his office by reason of age or infirmity".

speechtext: I do not think there ever was one.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
Irrespective of that consideration, Mr. Speaker, what this amendment really seeks, I repeat, so far as those who are now in office are concerned, is the summary removal of superior court judges over 75 years of age-if the amendment is carried -on March 1, 1961, even though they are not necessarily incapacitated or disabled from the due execution of their office. That is what the present amendment boils down to so far as the present superior court judges are concerned.
The Prime Minister himself has given us no facts, or very little to go on, that would justify, in our view, the action the government desires this parliament to take and desires the parliament of Westminster to take in respect of superior court judges who are now in office. I should like to say at once, however, that I am not objecting to 75 years as the retiring age for superior court judges. I have read the discussions on this matter that have taken place in the past. The Prime Minister referred to some of them. We have had great service in this country from judges over 75 years of age. However, I think there is a great deal to be said for abolishing life appointments of this kind and for setting an age limit, if you like to call it that, of 75 years. If this proposed amendment applied only to judges hereafter appointed, we on this side would not quarrel with this part of it at all.
But of course, as I have just said, this resolution goes much further. It turns out of office on March 1, 1961 all judges of these courts who have attained the age of 75 years. That, in our view, if I may use the words of Right Hon. R. B. Bennett on a similar occasion when there was discussion of this question, involves a breach of the contract between the individual who holds office at the
Amendment to B.N.A. Act present time and the state, because his patent of office declares that he shall hold office during life or good behaviour.
Those who accepted appointments to the superior courts, many of them no doubt at very considerable financial sacrifice, undoubtedly did so on the understanding that so long as they were able to carry out the duties for which they were appointed they would continue to hold judicial office.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman say whether the statement of Mr. Bennett was accepted by the Mackenzie King government?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
No, it was not. I am coming back to that, and I am glad the Prime Minister has brought it to my attention. Mr. Bennett's views were not accepted at that time, but I shall be glad to point out that in a subsequent session the government realized that perhaps it had gone too far in this matter and took steps to rectify the situation in so far as existing judges were concerned.
Judges of the superior court at that time had every reason to believe that the terms upon which they accepted office, which were set forth with such clarity in the British North America Act itself and which therefore gave those terms a special constitutional sanctity, would be maintained, or at least would not be changed unilaterally in this way. But now these judges are to be told that despite the formal declaration of their patent of office, which was based on an express provision of our constitution, they will after a certain date, having attained 75 years of age, cease to be judges.
Now I come to the point which the Prime Minister mentioned about the precedent I cited, in so far as I was quoting Mr. Bennett as a precedent. I fully realize that in 1927-the Prime Minister mentioned this himself-the parliament of Canada provided for the compulsory retirement at the age of 75 years of judges of the supreme court of Canada and of the exchequer court, even though appointed during good behaviour. That action by parliament was within the constitution and it was done-but as it cannot be done in this case-by legislation of the Canadian parliament. It was, however, as I have indicated, very strongly attacked by Mr. Cahan, who called it a serious breach of contract, and by Mr. Bennett. I would like to read what Mr. Bennett said about it, because it was Mr. Bennett's words and the attitude taken by the opposition at that time that were probably responsible for subsequent legislation which rectified the situation about which

Amendment to B.N.A. Act Mr. Bennett and Mr. Cahan had been particularly complaining. Mr. Bennett said in 1927, as reported on page 1556 of Hansard for that year:
-it will be remembered that under the British North America Act a judge is appointed during good behaviour or for life and when his commission is issued one of the terms of the commission is that very provision that he should hold office during good behaviour or life.
Then later he said:
I think we must have regard to the terms and conditions under which the original contract was made ... although it may seem out of the ordinary that a judge should draw full salary when he is retired compulsorily, nevertheless good faith and morals, in my judgment, impose upon us that obligation and it is an obligation which we should not lightly disregard.
Finally he said:
-I do not believe that the Canadian people would approve of our departing from the general principle that the government must-as in times past-have respect for the sanctity of a contract made between a servant of the crown when he entered the employment of the state . ..
If this bill applied only to future appointments, it would not be so objectionable.
The minister of justice of that day, Hon. Ernest Lapointe, at first did not accept this view, and the government proceeded to put the bill through. It was passed and compulsory retirement of the supreme court and exchequer court judges at age 75 was brought into effect. Later legislation was introduced, as the Minister of Justice no doubt knows, which provided that all judges who were affected by the 1927 legislation should be granted an annuity equal to their full salary at the time of retirement, and therefore no judge from that time on-I think it was in 1929 or 1930 that the change was made-suf-ferred in a financial way from that legislation.
Notwithstanding the stand taken especially by Mr. Bennett and Mr. Cahan, and the Conservative opposition in 1927, in 1933 the solicitor general of a Conservative administration, Hon. Maurice Dupre, introduced legislation which attempted to do by indirection what his party had previously condemned when they were in opposition, namely to force judges of the superior courts to retire at age 75; not by direct action such as we have before us today, but by introducing a provision which would have reduced their salaries when they reached age 75, thus perhaps making it desirable for them to retire at that age.
That legislation was introduced by the Conservative government of that time, and Mr. King and Mr. Lapointe, among others, took very strong exception to that particular bill. It was passed, however, in the House of Commons but was killed in the Senate,

notwithstanding an amendment moved by Mr. Jacobs, I think it was, to take the word "hereafter" out of the bill.
So, Mr. Speaker, we now have the situation that if this resolution is passed and this address is acted upon we will have a breach of contract with superior court judges. Because of that fact it is our duty to see that these new provisions regarding compulsory retirement should be made applicable only to those who are to be appointed hereafter as judges of superior courts. Knowing beforehand this limitation upon their tenure of office, those who are invited to become judges in the future can accept or refuse on the basis of those terms, and they would have no complaint if this action were taken.
May I call it one o'clock?
At one o'clock the house took recess.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
At the luncheon recess I was discussing the effect of his resolution on the tenure of office of judges of superior courts, and I was pointing out that if the resolution leads to an amendment of the British North America Act it will be a breach of contract in so far as these judges are concerned.
While I recognize that action of this kind was taken by a previous parliament in 1927 which dealt with the tenure of office and the compulsory retirement of judges of the supreme court and the exchequer court, apart from the fact that if that action was wrong then it is not right now, the government of that day did make provision to ensure that no judge was prejudiced financially by the action taken by parliament.
I realize that there is a resolution on the order paper which deals with pensions for superior court judges, and that some action may be taken by this government to deal with this question. I do not know what that action may be. It may be that provision will be made for a retirement allowance equal to the salary on retirement, or it may be judges will be granted the same kind of pension they would receive if they were retired for disability under the Judges Act. No doubt we will learn later what the government has in mind. But there is no question but that if this amendment to the act is made, judges who accepted office on certain conditions will be retired at 75, and this would be, I believe, a breach of contract.

There is a second question which arises, and that is the change which is proposed with regard to the procedure for removing district and county court judges. It is proposed in this resolution to request the addition to the British North America Act, that is to our constitution, of an express provision that judges of district and county courts shall, after September 1, 1960 according to the resolution and after March 1, 1961 according to the amendment, be removable only on an address of the Senate and House of Commons. The provision that county and the district court judges hold office during good behaviour is not, of course, in contrast to that affecting supreme court judges, to be found in the British North America Act. Their appointment has always been according to statutes of this parliament, which from time to time over the years have fixed the term of the appointment for as far back, if I am right, as 1882. Now it is proposed to change the procedure set forth in the Judges Act, which has remained substantially the same since parliament first legislated on this matter, and to substitute for the discreet but essentially fair process outlined in the Judges Act another procedure which apart from the fact that it will be enshrined in our constitution, would be characterized by great formality and, I believe, great publicity if it were ever adopted. Hereafter under this resolution, if the removal of a district or county court judge is sought for any reason, everything will have to be done under the spotlight that is always focused upon acts of parliament. There will be an atmosphere of unnecessary publicity, I think, for such an occasion.
It is essential of course that any proceedings, if they should ever be required, for the removal of a judge should be characterized by the greatest impartiality and justice, as I am sure they would be in any circumstances. But is it necessary that they should be carried out in what is bound to be distressing circumstances in the full glare of publicity which would attach to proceedings of this parliament? Surely our past experience in this country has been such that we can safely leave untouched what had been for many years, and still is, a satisfactory provision, even though the number of instances in which it has been applied is extremely limited if, indeed, it has been applied at all.
However, the government is going much further than merely changing the procedure to be followed if it proves necessary to remove a judge of a county or district court. This brings me to the third and last point I want to mention, and that concerns a further change which I think is altogether
Amendment to B.N.A. Act without precedent, namely a change which would fix in the British North America Act, in our constitution, the age for compulsory retirement of judges of district and county courts.
I do not know why the government is making this change in the constitution. The minister in the correspondence which has been tabled refers to serious doubts in regard to the constitutionality of action of this kind by the parliament of Canada. The Prime Minister has referred to the fact that the attorneys general of all the provinces have accepted the proposal, but there seems to be, at least in my mind, some ambiguity in regard to the acceptance of some of the attorneys general, or at least ambiguity in regard to the implications of the acceptance.
Turning to the appendix to Votes and Proceedings I find that the attorney general of British Columbia in his letter to the Minister of Justice, under date of November 4, 1959 said:
-I agree wholeheartedly with this recommendation and would go further to suggest that if it is not possible to secure the unanimous consent of all ten provinces that the act be made applicable to those provinces who have expressed approval of the legislation through their executive council.
The attorney general of Saskatchewan in his reply to the minister dated July 20, 1959 had this to say:
This government feels that it would prefer to have all provincial judges, including district court judges, retire at age 70 rather than age 75-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: Should the hon. member not read on?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
I will be glad to read on:
-but it is quite prepared to concur in an amendment to the British North America Act providing for superior court judges retiring at age 75 if the dominion and the other provinces are not prepared to concur in an amendment providing for their retirement at age 70.
We are proposing that this matter in regard to county court judges should be put in our constitution so that if in future any change of the kind suggested by the attorney general of Saskatchewan or the attorney general of any other province were desired it would have to be made by an amendment to the constitution, that is by going to the parliament of the United Kingdom.
The British North America Act in section 96 empowers the governor in council to appoint judges of the superior, district and county courts in each province except those of the courts of probate in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, but it is only with respect to superior court judges that the British North America Act provides for tenure during good behaviour, that is to say normally for life. That section contains no such provision

Amendment to B.N.A. Act for district and county court judges. Indeed, after providing for their appointment the act is silent concerning them.
There is only one reasonable deduction to be drawn from this; that the parliament of Canada was meant to have and indeed has had and has exercised the necessary legislature authority over the terms of appointment of district and county court judges. This is confirmed by precedent. These judges have been subjected, without any constitutional question being raised, to acts of this parliament providing for compulsory retirement, acts of this parliament going back as far as 1903,1 believe. Why is this change being made now?
There was a discussion of this matter in a debate in this house in 1927 to which I referred this morning. The then hon. member for Simcoe, Mr. Boys, a member of the opposition, as reported at page 1080 of the 1927 Hansard asked the following question of the then minister of justice, Mr. Lapointe:
Is there any special provision in the British North America Act with respect to the retirement of county court judges?
The then minister of justice replied "No", Mr. Boys went on to ask:
Is it suggested that such legislation-
That is, Canadian legislation for the compulsory retirement of county court judges.
-was ultra vires?
The then minister replied:
No, not at all. Section 99 applies only to the judges of the superior courts.
Mr. Lapointe went on to add:
There is nothing in the British North America Act preventing us from dealing with the tenure of office of county court judges.
Indeed the tenure of office of district and county court judges has long been established by federal statutes which parliament has been free to amend any time it saw fit without reference to any outside parliament. Now we propose to put it in the British North America Act that they must retire at 75. This will mean we will have to go to the parliament of the United Kingdom and ask it to amend our constitution accordingly in this matter. We are asked to accept the doctrine that henceforth any change in tenure of a district or county court judge would presumably not only have to be agreed to by every province but also by the parliament of the United Kingdom, which in the past has not been approached in these matters.
We are being told for instance I assume from this resolution, that while it is constitutional for the Canadian parliament under section 32 of the Judges Act to remove a district or county court judge for inability to perform his duties, it would be unconstitutional to remove him at the age of 75.

Therefore this address seeks to replace our parliament by the British parliament in regard to something which was never previously considered to be a function of any other parliament but our own. It was never previously considered by any government to be that, even by governments representing the party to which my hon, friend the Minister of Justice belongs.
By this resolution parliament is asking that its own power to deal with the tenure of office of district and county court judges be now limited by the constitution, and that action to bring about such limitation be taken by the parliament of the United Kingdom. In other words we are being asked in 1960 to expatriate to Westminster a part of our own constitution. I ask the minister, what kind of colonial vision is this? I ask him, if he can, to justify taking action of this kind at this time; to go to the parliament of the United Kingdom to make a change in our constitution through action of that parliament in a matter with which we in this parliament over the years since 1882 have managed to deal.
For this and for the other reasons I have mentioned I move, seconded by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), that the resolution be amended in proposed section 99 as follows:
That the words "district and county" be deleted from line two of subsection one; the words "district or county" and the word "whether" be deleted from line one of subsection two; the words "before or" be deleted from line two of subsection two, and all the words after the words "seventy five years" be deleted from subsection two.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks will be somewhat brief for reasons which are, of course, obvious. First of all, I do not consider myself an expert on constitutional matters. The second reason is that I have not had the time to work on this resolution as I should like to have done.
We have now reached the stage in the proceedings of this session where we have legislation, as one wit put it, by exhaustion. I am suffering from that and so are some other hon. members. Since the house rose at one o'clock I recorded a radio address to my constituents; I dictated several letters; I had an interview with two people and drank a hasty cup of coffee before coming down to the house. I mention that to you, sir, so that you will have some sympathy for members of this house who are plugging away under very difficult circumstances.
I might say that this group does support the purpose of this humble address which is to be presented to Her Majesty the Queen recommending certain amendments to the British North America Act. We support the

purpose because we believe the terms of the resolution are a progressive step toward a further recognition of Canada as a nation, and of changing circumstances.
However, I must say that we do wonder to some extent whether the amendment has been caused solely by the government's concern for the efficient administration of justice. While the principle and purpose of the amendment are quite good, we are not altogether lacking in suspicion as to the reason for its advancement; but no doubt the Minister of Justice will deal with the matter further when he rises to speak.
When I was listening to the Leader of the Opposition prior to the noon recess I was interested in his belabouring of the government; in his indication that the Liberals had recognized that Canada was a nation and that the amendment of the constitution should be within the confines of this country, and that Canada should not be required to seek the legislation through another parliament. I must bring this to his attention. If I heard him correctly he quoted the former prime minister, Mackenzie King, in this respect, and mentioned something about his hoping that constitutional changes would take place that would bring the amending of the constitution strictly within the powers of the Canadian parliament. But I must bring to your attention, Mr. Speaker, the fact that it was only a hope and that those words were uttered years ago. I must also bring to the attention of the house the fact that the Liberal party was in office for 22 years and that on this question, as on a good many questions, they hoped, but we did not get any action in that direction.
As compared with that, I want to bring to the attention of the house the policy of the C.C.F. The policy of the C.C.F. since its formation as a movement in 1932 has been that Canada as a self-governing nation should have the right to amend its own constitution without reference to another parliament. We recognize that these things cannot be done overnight, but I would challenge the Leader of the Opposition to bring to the house any evidence that the Liberal government took any steps in that direction, or any evidence of any conversations between former prime ministers and the appropriate persons in Great Britain with the end in view of changing the present practice so that Canada would have the right to change its own constitution. If there is that evidence I should be very willing to have it put forward, but I do not know of it. I just mention that point.
However, as far as this group are concerned, we have been advocating this change for years because, as I said before, we believe
Amendment to B.N.A. Act that Canada as a self-governing and independent nation should have the right to amend its own constitution. However when one considers and discusses this question I am sure that any fair person recognizes it is not all quite as simple and easy as it looks on the surface.
Now I deal with the resolution itself. Subsection 1 of the humble address reads as follows:
Subject to subsection 2 of this section, the judges of the superior, district and county courts shall hold office during good behaviour, but shall be removable by the governor general on address of the Senate and House of Commons.
While we support this section, I presume- and I am sure the Minister of Justice will correct me if I am wrong in this-that even prior to this amendment it was accepted throughout the years that the parliament of Canada had the right to take this action, although it was not so stated in the constitution. No doubt the Minister of Justice will inform us in that respect. However, we support this amendment and we believe it is better to put these powers in the constitution in language which is in exact terms. Subsection 2 reads:
A judge of a superior, district or county court, whether appointed before or after the coming into force of this section, shall cease to hold office upon attaining the age of seventy five years, or upon the coming into force of this section if at that time he has already attained that age.
We support this amendment; we believe it is a progressive amendment. In fact it is the type of amendment that has been suggested by the C.C.F. for many years. The question of the earlier retirement of justices and judges has been brought up in our conventions, from time to time. In saying this I am not intending to cast any reflection on the gentlemen of the bench, as I am sure there are many members of the legal profession who have a better knowledge of this than I have. I am just an ordinary peasant farmer living in the backwoods. But we are all subject to the effects of age. I have been in courts myself where I have noticed the justices. While they have had a very creditable past and were recognized as authorities, on account of age they were testy and impatient, and at times I thought they were somewhat unfair to the legal counsel when they were presenting their arguments. That is natural as a result of age, and I think on that account this is a good amendment.
Second, I think it is quite unfair that people who would not otherwise suffer financially should continue to hold these very important and highly placed positions until very late in life, and not leave the vacancies which would provide opportunities for many of the

Amendment to B.N.A. Act younger members of the legal profession, barristers and solicitors, to serve their country in that capacity.
I think it is a sound argument that at 75 years of age a person who is considered to have served his country well in such a capacity should retire. I must say that when I make these remarks I am not intending them to apply to the hon. member for Duf-ferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) as a member of parliament, because he is a rather exceptional person, always an ornament to the house. But I must say frankly that at times I am inclined to look at life in a personal way. I frankly say that I could miss his cheery countenance on the other side. He always inspires me to speak when I look at him.
For these two sound reasons, first, the facts of life so far as age is concerned and second, the provision of opportunities for younger members of the bar to occupy these very important positions, we support section 2 of the amendment. So we agree with the Prime Minister when he said this morning-when I say we agree with the Prime Minister I mean we believe what he said this morning is worthy of support, because there are occasions when we do not agree with the Prime Minister-if I heard him correctly, that age 75 was an appropriate time or anniversary for retiring. I think that was very well put, to make it a sort of farewell party at the same time.
In any event, for the reasons I have stated we support this humble address. I might say as well, Mr. Speaker, that I understand these honourable gentlemen, the justices and judges, are reasonably well provided for by way of pension, and that they have the opportunity of enjoying their pension anywhere in the world. They have had this opportunity since the establishment of the pension scheme. I understand also that the pension is on a noncontributory basis, a very interesting aspect, since it is a pension for life after retirement at about 50 per cent of the salary paid. Well, I believe that is a very reasonable provision for justices and judges when compared with the pensions received by many people when they retire. So, in supporting this legislation, we believe we are supporting something that is a step in the right direction, that will be to the advantage of efficiency in the administration of justice, and that will provide opportunities for younger members of the legal profession while at the same time not causing any injustice or hardship to the persons particularly affected.
I have not had an opportunity of reading the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition very carefully. I just hurriedly

consulted with the hon. member for Vancouver East before I rose and at this moment I would say on behalf of this group we are not inclined to support this amendment because we look upon it as a somewhat subtle attempt to emasculate the purpose of the legislation. That is all I have to say. (Translation):
Mr. Paul Mariineau (Ponliac-Temiscaminquek Mr. Speaker, I should like first to emphasize the vital importance of the duties performed by judges. On consideration, one realizes readily that in the administration of justice, judges carry out a mandate that derives from the Creator himself.
The early Romans had given justice a divine status, and even in our modern times, I think that justice must hold a very high rank, because it is the very basis of our society.
As the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) so rightly said this morning, we have been particularly fortunate in the choice of judges in this country. If the British system of justice is so highly regarded, not only in our country and in commonwealth countries, but throughout the world, it is due largely to the excellence of the judges who have presided over the various courts in Canada, or in Great Britain and in other commonwealth countries.
I should now like to consider some of the points raised by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson).
He said he is in favour of the retirement of judges at age 75 and, if I am not mistaken, he also favours compulsory retirement, because normally a man of 75 lacks the alertness and the working capacity of a younger man. I do not think anyone will deny that.
This does not mean, of course, that a person of 75 has outlived his usefulness to society.
Thinking of the plight that is now the lot of our older people, I remembered the words spoken a few days ago, in this building, by one of the most eminent Canadians we know, Dr. Wilder Penfield.
He has studied the psychological situation that each man has to face on reaching the age of retirement.
He said that a man who has reached 65, 70 or 75 certainly still had a contribution to make. Indeed he suggested that, when a man has reached the age of retirement, he should not confine himself to his room and patiently wait for the passing of the hours, the days and the years, waiting for death, but rather start on a second career. And that is the point I have in mind: a second career.
Is it not logical and normal that a man who has served his country with distinction in

the very significant office of a judge might, at age 75,-i.e. the limit established by the resolution-go on retirement but continue to serve his people in another occupation where his wealth of experience will be of great help to him? That is why I believe that the principle of compulsory retirement for judges is an excellent one.
The Leader of the Opposition said that compulsory retirement is a good thing, but that it should not apply to judges already appointed, because there is some kind of contract between the state, which appointed the judge, and the judge himself. In other words, if I rightly understood his argument, he thinks that, once appointed, a judge has a vested right to continue to occupy his post until death. But what would happen if a judge, because of his health, was unable to continue exercising his functions or, for some personal reasons-which I would not like to mention- did not like to give up his position? If some judges have to cease their functions at age 75, I say that they should all be treated equally. Otherwise, we would have a rather abnormal situation. There would be two kinds of judges, that is: newly appointed judges who, on reaching age 75, would have to retire under the terms of the address we are submitting to Her Majesty, and, on the other hand, judges who would continue in office.
I say that the personal interest of judges now in office should not have priority over the general welfare of this country. Moreover, as the opposition leader stated, a man having reached a certain age loses some of his faculties. When saying this, he only repeated certain truths which were advanced by the great philosophers of the past, including Aristotle who stated that, when he gets old, a man loses not only his physical but also his mental vigour-in any event he certainly loses some of his adaptability.
The rolls of courts today are increasingly heavy, and judges need not only particularly acute minds and great legal ability, but also great physical endurance if they are to go on giving their full measure.

In this respect, we agree: if some judges are to be retired, all should be.
The second point I want to raise is this. I do not see eye to eye with the Leader of the Opposition when he states that judges have a vested right, because that right entirely depends on the judge's ability to discharge
Amendment to B.N.A. Act the duties of his office. There is certainly no vested right for a judge.
The third point is that, according to the retirement system, a judge does not stand to lose much financially; in any case, he is in no way unfairly treated when he retires.

member-
