speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not discussing the details of a pension plan; I am merely saying that the judges who will be retired will come under a pension plan. Whether the plan is adequate or not-and I am convinced that it is, I do not wish to discuss the point, because I feel that it cannot be discussed in detail within the framework of this debate.
Therefore, from that standpoint, I certainly cannot accept the claims of the Leader of the Opposition.
The Leader of the Opposition also wondered why we had to proceed by way of a joint address of the house and the Senate to relieve a judge from his office. In my opinion, that system is the best, precisely because of the importance of the functions of a judge. And a judge should not be relieved of his office unless there are very serious reasons for it; besides, the very formalities attached to the procedure are a guarantee that it will not be lightly resorted to.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words about the address to be submitted to Her Majesty the Queen, in order to obtain a constitutional amendment.
The Prime Minister indicated this morning that since confederation-that is to say since 1867-there have been 17 occasions on which constitutional amendments were sought.
Today, another one is to be sought and we have not yet found a means that would meet the wish of everyone, that is to say, one that would allow us to amend our constitution ourselves. The Prime Minister said he hoped that, in the near future, some means could be found to completely repatriate our constitution, so that we would not have to resort to the services of a parliament of another country to amend our constitution as we see fit.
It is true that the restriction to the sovereignty or total independence of our country

Amendment to B.N.A. Act
is a result of the very will of the Canadian government, of the people of Canada. However, we hope, Mr. Speaker, that this anomaly may soon be removed. I feel this is a matter which goes beyond the scope of a political debate, and that the most enlightened efforts, wills and brains of this country should strive to achieve that end.
Mr. Speaker, everybody knows that in a few years, our country will celebrate the centenary of its foundation. Would it not be a lofty objective, one worthy of our energies and our hope that, by that time, an agreement acceptable to all sections of our population, to all governments and to all ethnic groups will be entered into which will bring understanding between those various groups? Would this not indicate that our country has attained maturity?
It is not a matter of putting forward strict and dogmatic amendments; what is required is that discussions be held between groups to achieve a goal that everyone considers desirable.
This goal is surely not impracticable, and I remember that during his recent visit to Canada, General De Gaulle said something which struck me very much. He said that he had faith in the ability of human beings to find answer to their problems. In other words, he believes there is no problem, however serious, that cannot be solved by the concerted good will of men.
Mr. Speaker, I respectfully submit that it is with that attitude that we should approach this problem of the repatriation of the constitution which, I admit, is quite serious and is bound to interest all groups in our country.
Mr. Speaker, I am glad of having had the opportunity, during the debate on this resolution, to suggest the attitude we must take and that will surely lead us to the solution of the problem of the repatriation of the constitution.

Mr. Speaker, while listening to the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue, (Mr. Martineau), I was rather

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. That is not at all what I suggested. maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my statement and the correction made by the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscaminque amount practically to the same thing. The purpose is exactly the same.
May I remind him of this: there may be exceptions, cases where mental powers grow less, where the brain is less active, but this is not necessarily the case with everybody. I only wish to give a few examples.
Let us take the case of Dr. Penfield himself. Is there anyone with a more alert intelligence than Dr. Penfield? Yet he is over 70. John XXIII has been elected pope at the age of 78. Was he so elected because the church considered him an inadequate representative.
We have seen in the past-

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: Is the hon. member aware that Dr. Penfield recently retired and is starting on a second career, that of a writer?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
He has a perfect right to do so, but it should not stop him from availing himself of the privilege of continuing in the same field. He has enough knowledge and ability to do so.
Let us, for instance, take the case of Leo XIII, who was made pope at the age of 73 and remained in that high office until he was

93. He was recognized as an authority, not only in his time, but of all times. The encyclicals he wrote when he was 90 are still outstandingly valid today.
Let us now examine the case of Sir Thomas Chapais who, until the age of 93, was considered an outstanding authority in the field of Canadian history.
Therefore, that matter of lessened mental power cannot be made a general rule.
I admit it would be preferable, as Dr. Pen-field said, that a man, at a certain age, should quit his regular occupations and enjoy leisure, or take up some hobby. On this I agree with the hon. member, but we cannot accept that, in general, a man's faculties dwindle with age. At least, if it is so for some people, I hope it will not happen to the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue or to myself. I hope to live beyond age 75.
Mr. Speaker, I did not rise only to say this to the hon. member. I simply wanted to say that, in my opinion, this is a backward resolution. We are losing ground instead of going forward. If we look into the history of our country, more particularly since 1887, we see that at all times we have striven to secure independence from the government in the British Isles.
In 1897, at the time of Queen Victoria's jubilee, Sir Wilfrid Laurier in a memorable speech, asked the British government to give more latitude to the governments of the dominions, which needed it to reach their full expansion. He was supported in this by General Smuts, of South Africa.
Later, in 1918, Sir Robert Borden insisted that Canada, which had taken part in the 1914-18 war, and which was still a colony at the time, be made a party to the Versailles treaty, and he signed that treaty on behalf of Canada. It was another step towards our independence.
In 1921, I believe, the Hon. Ernest Lapointe signed a fisheries treaty with the United States and, at the time, objected to the presence of a representative from the London government.
In 1927, the Right Hon. Mackenzie King set up the basis of what later on was to become the treaty of Westminster, in order to confer greater authority to Canada, and a greater measure of autonomy.
In 1931, Mr. Bennett signed this treaty of Westminster which granted us complete freedom and a status of equality with the London government. Later, the government eliminated appeals to the privy council and decided that the Queen would no longer be
Amendment to B.N.A. Act sovereign of England and the dominions, but the Queen of Canada, our own sovereign and not just the Queen of England. Those are the moves we have made since confederation and it shows we have always aimed at greater independence.
And now, this government is again going to ask London permission to do this or that. It will be said: "Oh, it is because this matter is not clear," as the Prime Minister said this morning.
If it is not clear, if there is some doubt, why do we not get the benefit of the doubt?
Besides, if we refer to the British North America Act, we see that in the field of exclusive powers of provincial legislatures, section 92, paragraph 16, says the following:
Generally all matters of a merely local or private nature in the province.
I admit that what is specified there as far as the provinces are concerned, is not specified from a federal point of view. We see there an indication that what is allowed in matters of a purely local or provincial nature should by that very fact, be allowed in matters of purely national nature. Reference to the Quebec resolutions will show that it was the intent of the fathers of confederation to establish that the federal government would have the exclusive right to legislate of itself in purely federal matters.
In paragraph 37, section 29, of the Quebec Resolutions, we note the following:
And generally respecting all matters of a general character, not specially and exclusively reserved for the local governments and legislatures.
That proves, therefore, that the fathers of confederation wished that it be so, and that if that does not appear in the British North America Act proper, it is because it had been felt it was so clear that it was not necessary to include it.
Later, in the London Resolutions, paragraph 36, section 28, we note the following:
And generally respecting all matters of a general character not specially and exclusively reserved for the local legislatures.
It may be inferred from the thinking of the fathers of confederation, at the time the discussions took place, either at Quebec or in London, that it was their wish to reserve to the various governments the various rights which were theirs.
The governments of the provinces, as I said a moment ago, in quoting section 92, have the right, in purely provincial matters, to legislate for themselves, in their own province, at any time. In reading over the report of the Quebec and London discussions, we realize that it was the intention of the

Amendment to B.N.A. Act lathers of confederation to grant that same privilege to the federal government, in purely national and federal matters.
I admit that where there is a dual character, that is a federal one and a provincial one, we might perhaps have the right-it seems to me, after a century, now that the Canadian nation has reached maturity, now that it is 93 years old-to be in a position to settle our own problems by ourselves.
I know Eight Hon. Mr. St. Laurent wanted to repatriate the constitution altogether in 1949, but the Quebec government opposed the move, claiming it feared the federalists. Well, there are those matters of a dual character, federal and provincial, which must still be submitted to the London government, for settlement. Besides, the sections of the B.N.A. Act, which I have quoted, seem to indicate that it was clearly the aim of the fathers of confederation to leave to the federal government and to the provincial governments the care of settling their own respective problems.
Now, if we examine the Statute of Westminster, which granted full freedom to Canada and to the other dominions of the time, we see in the third paragraph of the preamble the following:
Whereas it is in accord with the established constitutional position that no law hereafter made by the parliament of the United Kingdom shall extend to any of the said dominions as part of the law of that dominion otherwise than at the request and with the consent of that dominion.
Therefore, if we want to take a backward step, we may do so; if we want to go to London and ask the people there to render a judgment, to adopt a law, we can do so, but it is only at our request that it can be done. But if we are not compelled to do so, why should the government, seeing that all other governments, even Conservative, have sought to achieve greater freedom, take a retrograde step and ask the London government today to legislate in its stead? Section 2 reads as follows:
The Colonial Laws Validity Act, 1865, shall not apply to any law made after the commencement of this act by the parliament of a dominion.
And paragraph 2 of that section reads as follows:
No law and no provision of any law made after the commencement of this act by the parliament of a dominion shall be void or inoperative on the ground that it is repugnant to the law of England, or to the provisions of any existing or future act of parliament of the United Kingdom, or to any order, rule, or regulation made under any such act, and the powers of the parliament of a dominion shall include the power to repeal or amend any such act, order, rule or regulation in so far as the same is part of the law of the dominion.

Any parliament can repeal, modify or improve legislation, without having to go to London. And the Statute of Westminster gives us the most absolute independence, as stated in section 2.
And in section 3, what do we see?
It is hereby declared and enacted that the parliament of a dominion has full power to make laws having extra-territorial operation.
And section 4 tells us:
No act of parliament of the United Kingdom passed after the commencement of this act shall extend or be deemed to extend, to a dominion as part of the law of that dominion, unless it is expressly declared in that act that that dominion has requested, and consented to, the enactment thereof.
It is therefore the dominion government that may do the asking; and never the London government. If it wants to take a retrograde step, that is its own business. It has the right to ask London to legislate on behalf of Canada. But, in my opinion, that would be a backward step. We should not go back to colonialism, under which we were governed before the Statute of Westminster. I suggest that no truly Canadian government has the right to take such a retrograde step; it should settle that problem itself, since this is a purely national problem, coming within the scope of its own responsibility.
And here is what we read in section 6 of the Statute of Westminster:
Without prejudice to a generality of the foregoing provision of this act, and as soon as the latter is in force, they must cease to be in effect in the dominions, section four of the Colonial
And section 7 reads as follows:
Courts of Admiralty Act-
(1)	Nothing in this act shall be deemed to apply to the repeal, amendment or alteration of the British North America Acts, 1867 to 1930, or any order, rule or regulation made thereunder.
(2)	The provisions of section two of this act shall extend to laws made by any of the provinces of Canada and to the powers of the legislatures of such provinces.
(3)	The powers conferred by this act upon the Parliament of Canada or upon the legislatures of the provinces shall be restricted to the enactment of laws in relation to matters within the competence of the parliament of Canada or of any of the legislatures of the provinces respectively.
Therefore, as regards matters within national or provincial jurisdiction, it is the government of Ottawa and the provincial governments which have the authority to legislate.
Is the matter now being considered a concern of ours as members of the federal parliament, or does it come under provincial

jurisdiction? If it is a matter for the federal government, I do not see why we should be going to London for permission to do something that is already granted to us under the Statute of Westminster and, by inference, in the British North America Act.
In my opinion, we have no right to allow the government of Canada to take this backward step.

In answer to the hon. member, I must say that, as far as courts of justice are concerned, there are strictly provincial courts, such as magistrate and municipal courts.
A few years ago, someone went so far as to question the right of provinces to establish such courts. It was being claimed that under the British North America Act the field of justice should be left entirely to the federal government.
But following an agreement between the provincial and federal governments, those courts were allowed to be established and, since that time, this legislation has been disregarded. However, there are still certain jurists who believe that the provinces have no right to establish those courts of justice.

Does the hon. member know that the administration of the superior court, in the province of Quebec, comes under provincial jurisdiction, even if the judges of that court are appointed by the federal government?

speechtext: The appointments-

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT

speechtext:
I think that part of the administration comes under provincial jurisdiction, but the appointments themselves are made by the federal government.
There is a definite relation between the appointment and the retirement of a person. The same government is responsible for appointing and retiring a judge.
Since the present act seeks to establish that judges may be retired at age 75, I suggest that this bill, which deals particularly with their removal or retirement, is of a general character and that we have a right to legislate in this matter, without any reference to the parliament in London.
Section 11 reads as follows:
Notwithstanding anything in the Interpretation Act, 1889, the expression "colony" shall not, in any act of the Parliament of the United Kingdom passed after the commencement of this act, include a dominion or any province or state forming part of a dominion.
That is clearly to establish that we got rid of our colonial status in 1931, when the treaty of Westminster was signed.
Mr. Speaker, now that Canada has gained international status, now that it is a member state of the United Nations in its own right and not as a member of the British empire, and also a member of NATO in its own right, and not as part of the British empire, I maintain that the action now taken by this government is a step backward and that we have no right to let it be so.
If we want to legislate in this matter, the government may, if it sees fit, establish that judges are to be retired at age 75.
However, there are men who, at 75, have acquired a rare maturity, a very sound judgment, and who are endowed with a physical energy which enables them to continue in office. But-and that is the point I want to stress-if the legislation were to pass here in Canada the London parliament should not be asked to legislate in a field which is our own concern.
That is why I favour the proposed amendment, because I am satisfied that it would benefit Canada and safeguard our independence.

Mr. Speaker, I should like at the outset to establish that in speaking now I will be speaking to the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) because I

Amendment to B.N.A. Act should like to deal with that matter inasmuch as the hon. gentleman did advance some arguments that require to be dealt with. As Your Honour knows, however, I do have to move an amendment myself and I should like to have it clear therefore that in speaking now I am speaking to the amendment of the Leader of the Opposition. At a later stage I will speak, I expect very briefly, mainly to move the amendment that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) indicated this morning should be moved.
I am certain that all hon. members appreciate and certainly I appreciate the spirit in which this subject has been approached by the hon. members who have taken part in this debate. Indeed, I appreciate very much the constructive if critical approach of the Leader of the Opposition to the resolution now before the house. With regard to his remarks concerning the position in connection with constitutional amendments generally, I think it is correct to say that there is no disagreement in principle between this side of the house and that side of the house. In fact, I thought I detected a substantial measure of agreement between what the Prime Minister had to say and what the Leader of the Opposition had to say in that regard.
This is not, it seems to me, a matter upon which one should indulge in a betting or racing contest. I know that when my hon. friends opposite had responsibility of office they made sincere and conscientious efforts to find a method under which, by general agreement, the constitution could be repatriated, brought home to Canada and made capable of amendment in Canada. It is true that on occasion one seeks to make political capital out of the failure of his opponents to solve the problems that confront us. But I think in this connection one should attempt- although one is not always successful at least one should attempt-to resist that temptation and approach this subject as I do on the basis that if my hon. friends were not successful that was something to be regretted by us indeed as much as by them.
With respect to this subject, this is an attempt that we intend to carry on sincerely and conscientiously. We have hopes of success. All I can say at the moment, however, is that we are working on that subject and that at a time when it seems appropriate, when we have been able to record some progress, then the Prime Minister will announce to the house what progress has been made. So with respect to the question of the

constitutional amendment itself I am not going to go into detail because I think that at least in principle and with respect to objective there is no disagreement between us. I should like therefore to confine the detail of my remarks to the arguments and criticisms advanced by the Leader of the Opposition with respect to the resolution itself.
The resolution, if I apprehended the hon. gentleman's remarks correctly, was criticized on three main grounds by the Leader of the Opposition and I shall deal with his three chief criticisms in a moment. But before making those criticisms the hon. member raised a general question, which was: Is there any urgency with respect to this proposal? As the hon. gentleman said, "Here you are amending the constitution; you are still having to do it in the old and time-honoured method by an address to Her Majesty praying that she will cause the United Kingdom parliament to take certain action," and therefore as the hon. gentleman said and I think quite properly, "you must be satisfied that there is urgency about the question when you are asking parliament to adopt such a resolution."
I should like then to deal briefly with the question of urgency. I think there is urgency about this and I believe the question of urgency can be answered on three grounds. First, there are the requests that have come from people who are outside the House of Commons and the government, but who are concerned with the position of the judiciary. Second, there are the efforts that have been made over the years to find some method of achieving this result, that is bringing about a situation under which the judges of superior courts will be retired at 75. Third, there is the fact that for the first time in the history of this matter we now have agreement of all the ten provinces that in fact this proposal should be put forward.

The first ground on which I say there is urgency is that of an analysis of the requests received from persons and bodies outside parliament and the government itself. I have here a list of the various occasions on which the Canadian Bar Association has

requested such action. It may go back further than the period covered by my list but mine goes back as far as 1936 when there was a resolution of the council of the Canadian Bar Association urging upon the minister of justice to adopt the necessary means to put into effect the principle, and I quote:
[DOT]-that a judge should generally retire when reaching the age of 75 years.
Then, in 1937, a report of the committee on the administration of civil justice of the Canadian Bar Association included the recommendation that the judges of superior courts of provinces should be subject to the same compulsory retirement rules as judges of the federal and county courts. In 1944 a resolution of the Ontario section of the Canadian Bar Association urged the establishment of a compulsory retirement age of superior court judges at 75. In June, 1952 there was a letter from the president of the Canadian Bar Association requesting the consideration of the requirement of judges of superior courts at 75; in 1953 a letter from the president of the Canadian Bar Association expressed the hope that the necessary amendment to the British North America Act would be passed soon. That was January 23, 1953.
On September 12, 1953 a resolution of the Canadian Bar Association urged the government of Canada to take the necessary step to bring about the compulsory retirement of superior court judges at the age of 75. Then on March 10, 1955 there was a letter from the president of the Canadian Bar Association, on behalf of the council of the bar, urging generally that action be taken to deal with this matter. The most recent one is the resolution of the annual meeting of the Canadian Bar Association in Vancouver on September 4, 1959, reading as follows:
Resolved that the Canadian Bar Association reiterates its recommendation for the compulsory retirement of superior court judges at the age of 75 years, and suggests that the question whether parliament has under the British North America Act No. 2, 1949, power to amend the constitution of Canada to so provide be submitted to the Supreme Court of Canada.
So, Mr. Speaker, over the period of years, at least from 1936 until the present, there have been no fewer than eight submissions from the governing body of the bar of Canada urging that the parliament of Canada take action to deal with this problem and to provide for a retirement age of judges of the superior courts at 75 years.

Quite so. I am dealing now with the general question raised by the Leader of the Opposition as to whether there is urgency to deal with this matter. I think that what
Amendment to B.N.A. Act I have said establishes that, in the view of that organization, which apart from parliament itself is most responsible and has most responsibility as well as authority in this matter, it is a very urgent problem.
The second ground upon which I say the question of urgency raised is completely answered is the history of the efforts over the years to deal with this matter. Surely it would be agreed by my hon. friends opposite that if there was no urgency, governments of which they have been members and which their party has supported over the years would not have made the quite strenuous efforts which have been made to deal with this problem and find a solution of it. This, however, is the fact; the governments of which my hon. friends were supporters and of which some of my hon. friends were members, have made conscientious efforts to find a solution to this problem. It is a fact also that the solution which my hon. friends thought was the proper one when they had the responsibility, was to bring forward an amendment to the British North America Act to provide, with the consent of the provinces, that there should be inserted an amendment to section 99 of that act providing for compulsory retirement of superior court judges on reaching the age of 75.
Reference was made in passing by the Prime Minister this morning to some of those attempts. Perhaps I could just add some details. Not every attempt in this field has been by way of amendment of the British North America Act but I think the majority of them-and certainly the sound ones-have been along those lines. In 1920 consideration was given to the amendment of the British North America Act to provide for removal of judges by the governor in council upon the finding of a commission of inquiry that a judge was disabled from the due execution of his office by reason of age or permanent infirmity. Indeed, in 1920, the then minister of justice-and this, of course, was a Conservative minister of justice-introduced a resolution to this effect which, however, remained on the order paper all during that session and was not dealt with.
Then in 1926-27 there was the provision which has been referred to this morning dealing, of course, only with the Supreme Court of Canada and the exchequer court and not requiring a constitutional amendment. In 1933, as the Leader of the Opposition pointed out, there was what perhaps might be fairly described as an attempt to overcome the difficulty of the constitutional amendment and find another method of providing in effect for the retirement of judges of superior courts. That bill, although passed by the House of Commons, was defeated in the Senate.

Amendment to B.N.A. Act
Then in 1936 I am informed a bill was drafted giving superior court judges who had served 20 years or more and who resigned at 75 an annuity equal to their salaries, but nothing came of it.
In 1944 there was a further attempt by way of a private bill introduced by Mr. Stanley Knowles, on the same lines as the 1933 bill, except the retirement on salary would have applied at the age of 70 instead of 75. That bill did not pass the House of Commons.
In 1945 the then minister of justice, the Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent, made an attempt to reach an agreement with the provinces on this matter. On January 2, 1945 he wrote to the attorney general of each province suggesting for his consideration an amendment to the British North America Act to provide for the retirement of superior court judges upon reaching a certain age. He suggested that the matter should be brought up at the next dominion-provincial conference. Replies were received from six of the provinces, and there is a letter on file indicating the matter was placed on the agenda. However, at that time Alberta disagreed with the whole method of amending the constitution and wished to discuss this question in full. No replies seem to have been received from the provinces of British Columbia, Saskatchewan and Nova Scotia. My hon. friends will find a full statement by Mr. St. Laurent reported at page 2711 of the House of Commons debates for 1946, in which he outlined his attempts to get agreement on this matter and to have it discussed, and reported the failure of those efforts.
A further attempt was made in 1955 by my immediate predecessor in the position of minister of justice when Mr. Garson urged the Canadian Bar Asociation to suggest to the provincial attorneys general that they might co-operate with the government of Canada on this matter. The results of those efforts are recorded in a letter from the then president of the Canadian Bar Association to Mr. Garson, dated March 10, 1955, in which the president reported that all the provincial vice presidents had been in touch with the attorneys general of their respective provinces, and he records the result which again unfortunately was lack of unanimity. That letter from the then president of the Canadian Bar Association concludes with these two paragraphs:
I have found that the members of the association all across Canada consider that this matter is an urgent one and that, in the interests of the administration of justice, action is required thereon.
I would bespeak your early consideration of the earlier and continuing recommendation of the Canadian Bar Association.

There have been a variety of requests. However, the majority of them have recognized that amendment of the British North America Act is the proper method of bringing about this result. There are other letters which merely refer generally to the desirability of bringing about the retirement of judges of superior courts at age 75.
The last recommendation from the bar association, that is the one of 1959 to which I referred earlier, recognized that an amendment to the British North America Act is essential, and actually suggested that this question be referred to the Supreme Court of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
I will come to the question of district and county court judges, in the course of my reply to one or two points made by the Leader of the Opposition. I am dealing, at this time, only with the question of urgency of the provision of a retirement age of 75 for superior court judges. I have, I believe, covered the second point in answer to the question of urgency, the answer which is given by the number of attempts made by governments over the years in Canada to find a formula under which this might be accomplished.
The third ground of urgency as to why this proposal should be put forward now and why the government urges upon parliament that it should adopt the resolution presenting the address is that for the first time in the history of this matter we do now have the unanimous consent of all ten provinces. This is the first time that has occurred during a period extending back at least as far as 1936, if not farther than that. I am not going to attempt to lay down any constitutional principle here, but I do suggest to my hon. friends that since governments are not bound

by decisions of previous governments with respect to matters of this kind, I am not at all certain that it would be proper for me to obtain the consent of a province to a certain proposal in 1959, shall we say, and then not act upon that proposal until perhaps 1961. In my view, I am under an obligation to act promptly, and in so far as we present to parliament the consent of the provincial governments as a basis for what we are asking parliament to do, then I think parliament should proceed on the basis that it must act with reasonable expedition with respect to the proposal to which the provincial governments have consented.
I do not believe it would be a proper thing for a minister of justice, or a prime minister, to come before parliament two or three years from now and say, we had the consent of all the provincial governments back in 1959, so we are asking parliament now to act upon that consent or to act with the knowledge of that consent. My position is not to attempt to lay down any constitutional principles on this point; but my position is simply that as a responsible minister and a minister who expects to have good relations and businesslike relations with the ministers of provincial governments with whom I deal I cannot too long delay acting in accordance with the consent I have received. I do not believe good relations could be furthered or maintained if one were to wait for more than a reasonable period and then, without going back to the provinces, come before parliament and say that we did have the consent of the ten provinces.
I suggest to parliament, therefore, that having now for the first time in the history of this subject obtained the unanimous consent of the ten provinces, having it established as I conceive it to be established that this is a sound, desirable proposition, it is then incumbent upon parliament in the national interest to deal with the proposition while that consent of the provinces is real consent in the sense that it has recently been given.
I am quite certain I do not need to labour the point. All hon. members would agree with me that it would be, if not a breach of faith at least a straining of good relations, if we were to allow this matter to lie over for another year or two years and then attempt to deal with it, without going back to all the provinces to ascertain if they were of the same view as they had expressed in the latter part of 1959 when they consented to this proposal. I do state quite emphatically and categorically, Mr. Speaker, that it seems to me the question of urgency raised by the Leader of the Opposition is effectively answered on the three grounds I have advanced.
Amendment to B.N.A. Act
I should like, then, to go to the three specific criticisms that he made of the proposal contained in the address which we are asking parliament to adopt. One was that what is involved here amounts to a breach of contract with respect to the judges who have been appointed to office before this resolution is adopted by parliament. The second point was that he objected to the equation of district and county court judges on the one hand with superior court judges on the other in the resolution and the proposed address. The third point was that he criticized us for including the position of county and district court judges, in effect, under the constitution of Canada instead of leaving them where they have been in the past, in his submission, to be dealt with exclusively under the Judges Act with respect to their tenure of office.
I should like to leave the first point to the end because it seemed to me to be the most important of the points raised by the Leader of the Opposition, and go directly to the second point in which, if I understood him correctly, he objected to the equation of district and county court judges on the one hand with superior court judges on the other in so far as their tenure of office is concerned. In answer to this criticism I would point out to you, Mr. Speaker, that in my view this is a very proper equation to make. The only provision for retirement of county court judges at the present time is found in sections 31 to 33 of the Judges Act. This is a very difficult, far-reaching, and indeed I might almost say terrible procedure. This provision calls for the appointment of a commission by the minister of justice to inquire into the question of whether or not a judge has become incapacitated or disabled from the due execution of his office by reason of age or infirmity. Then, sections 32 and 33 provide for the carrying on of that commission of inquiry, for the laying of the report before parliament.
This, I have described, as a very terrible method of procedure and one that, to my knowledge, if I recollect correctly, has only been resorted to once in the whole history of Canada. If I understand it correctly, this is the only procedure available at the present time for the removal from office of a district or county court judge prior to his reaching the age of 75 years.
It is true that the constitution does give the government or rather the governor general the power to appoint a district, county or superior court judge under section 96, but the constitution is silent on the removal of district and county court judges. Section 99 does provide for the removal of superior court judges. This is the reason I say that at the present time the only method of removal of

Amendment to B.N.A. Act county or district court judges, prior to reaching the age of 75 years when they automatically retire, is this very difficult and terrible provision under the Judges Act.
This situation, however, does not apply to superior court judges. In so far as superior court judges are concerned, there are three ways by which they can be removed from office at the present time. The first is by virtue of the provisions of section 99 which mentions good behaviour. There could be a court action bringing into question the good behaviour of a judge and calling for his removal; that would be the first method. Second, there is the simple method of an address of both houses of parliament, and I shall have more to say about this in connection with the alleged breach of contract. As I have said, section 99 provides that superior court judges can be removed by an address of both houses, and that is the second method.
I said there were three methods by which we could at the present time remove superior court judges, but actually we are providing the third method by this proposed address; that is that by the limitation on their age they will be removable or will cease to hold office at age 75 years. If therefore we did not include district and county court judges under the same general provisions we would have in effect only two methods of removing these judges whereas we would have three methods of removing superior court judges.
The other important feature to be considered in this connection is that we would not have provided for district and county court judges any security of office. They would not be appointed to hold office during good behaviour. There is an interesting comparison between the position of district and county court judges now and the position of superior court judges. Section 99 of the British North America Act provides that the judges of the superior courts shall hold office during good behaviour. It makes no mention whatsoever of the judges of district or county courts. It therefore seems to us to be entirely defensible that when we are instituting the last provision or the ultimate provision which now will make all judges appointed by the federal authority subject to termination of office at the age 75 years, that we should equate the conditions under which they hold their office, one with the other. It is therefore a perfectly proper and indeed a desirable thing that the conditions of tenure of office as well as the circumstances regarding the removal from office of district and county court judges on the one hand should be equated to and made similar with those conditions applicable to superior court judges

on the other. We therefore propose to amend the constitution in order to make the situation clear.
With regard to the question of why it is desirable to place the district and county court judges provision in the constitution, may I point out that, as my letters to the provinces which are on record have indicated, it is our view that there is a question as to the constitutional validity of that provision of the Judges Act which now provides that county court judges should retire at age 75 years. May I point out that under section 92(14) of the British North America Act the provinces are given exclusive authority over the administration of justice in the province, including the constitution, maintenance and organization of provincial courts, both of civil and of criminal jurisdiction. In those provinces which have county and district courts the organization, constitution and authority of those courts are matters to be dealt with by the provinces in exactly the same way and to exactly the same extent, so far as I have been able to appreciate, as is the case with the superior courts. Both courts are regulated, organized and have their jurisdictions established by the provinces. It seems to me that the courts at both levels have their organization and jurisdiction established under the authority conferred on the provinces by section 92(14). If that be the case, then it seems to me to be an anomaly, and to raise a serious question as to why, if it requires a constitutional amendment, as I believe it does, to impose a retirement age of 75 years on judges of superior courts, it does not take the same sort of amendment to impose that same retirement age on county court judges.

speechtext: Because of the importance of this matter and because of the long standing practice on the part of all governments, has my hon. friend been able to find in the departmental tiles any suggestion on the part of his predecessor that there was in the British North America Act any implication that would warrant the interpretation with regard to district court judges that the Minister of Justice has given us this afternoon?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: Yes. I have discussed this matter at great length with my departmental officials because I realize that what I am doing is not to be lightly done. That is the view of my advisers. I do not wish to shelter behind their opinion or in any way to suggest that the responsibility is theirs. It is my view which coincides entirely with theirs-or shall I put it the other way, that their view coincides entirely with mine-and upon which I am resting my case here in the House of Commons this afternoon, that while the provision has not been challenged in the courts, it is true, there is involved a residual doubt as to the authority of this parliament to impose a retiring age on a judge of a county court, which court is organized and constituted by a province. speechtext:
Perhaps I should ask to be allowed to answer that question at the conclusion of my remarks and in the meantime I will get the authoritative information.
Having attempted and, I believe, having succeeded in establishing the desirability on constitutional grounds of making the same provision with respect to county and district court judges as is made in respect to superior court judges, may I deal with the third point made by the Leader of the Opposition, namely that this is a constitutionally regressive step. The Leader of the Opposition said that to enact now a constitutional amendment providing the retirement age of 75 years for district and county court judges means that if you want to change that retiring age, it will be necessary to go to the United Kingdom parliament for that change whereas, previously, when the authority for district and county court judges retirement age rested in the Judges Act it was not necessary to refer the matter to the United Kingdom parliament if you wanted to change that age.
With the facts of the argument I have no quarrel. It is quite true that if we now embody in the constitution a provision governing the retirement age for county court judges, we can only change it by further constitutional amendment. But again I think this is a desirable feature; and I think it is also desirable that the retirement age for superior court judges should be in the constitution rather than elsewhere. The reason is this. There has been criticism advanced in the country, criticism which must be dealt with, that parliament is being asked here by the government to make an attack upon and to remove the basis of the independence of the judiciary; that this is just the opening wedge for interference by the government with the judiciary because-this criticism runs-the government is now saying to parliament that with respect to those who have previously enjoyed a life tenure of office that tenure is now ended at 75 years of age.
Mr. Speaker, this is not in my view a criticism which can be substantiated because I do not think anyone disagrees with the principle that judges should be retired at 75. I do not think it has to be met on that ground, but perhaps it should be met on the ground that this is not giving the government as such-the executive-the right to determine the conditions under which judges will hold office or under which they will leave office.

Amendment to B.N.A. Act
I think it would have been most undesirable had we adopted one course which might have been adopted, and that is to ask for a constitutional amendment conferring upon the government of Canada the right to determine the retirement age.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: That is what you should have done.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
That is not what we should have done. We were urged in some quarters to do this, and not to put the age in the amendment itself but to ask for an amendment which would say that the government or the governor in council or parliament may determine the retiring age of the judges. Hon. members are familiar with all the arguments in that regard and the argument as to whether or not it is more difficult to get a constitutional amendment than it is to get a bill through parliament. But by enshrining it in the constitution, I say that we have taken advantage of all the arguments made by my hon. friends and others in other spheres, that we are placing beyond the whim and reach of the government of the day the right to determine what shall be the retiring age. We can now only change this retiring age by asking parliament to enact a further constitutional amendment, and we do it this way quite deliberately simply because we think it is important that the principle should be maintained, that it is not this government or this parliament alone which determines the retirement age of judges of provincial courts. Since the judiciary is in fact established under the constitution, and the relationship between the judiciary, the executive and the legislatures is established by the British North America Act itself, we feel that this change and further changes as important as this should be made only as the result of a constitutional amendment and not placed within the reach of the unfettered legislative authority of one of the legislatures which make up the total of legislative authority in Canada.
That seems to me to be a very good reason for enshrining the age limit with regard to county and district court as well as superior court judges in the constitution. This, of course, is quite different from the case of the Supreme Court of Canada and the Exchequer Court of Canada. Those courts are creatures of the federal parliament exclusively. Their judges are not, as in the case of district, county and superior courts, joint responsibilities in the sense of being appointed under the federal authority in Canada to courts established under the authority of the legislature of a province. So we believe it to be quite sound to place the retirement ages of all judges of such courts in the


constitution rather than under the legislative authority of the dominion parliament alone.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the minister but his time has expired.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, surely the minister is replying to what could be regarded as a vote of want of confidence and therefore has unlimited time.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: I think it would be preferable, rather than discuss the point raised by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate for the house to give consent to the minister continuing his remarks.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: Agreed.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
May I ask the
minister, before he goes on, if he could tell us how many superior court judges and how many district court judges it is estimated will be affected as a result of the completed act?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
Yes; may I answer that now. District court judges will not be affected at all because they already have a retirement age; we are merely continuing that by the address. With regard to superior court judges I think the figure is 12, but I have it here and I will give an authoritative answer later. That is, there are 12 who are now 75 or will be 75 by March 1, 1961.
I appreciate what the house has done with respect to extension of time, if it be an extension. I have a third point to deal with and I shall be as brief as I can, but I think it is the most important point, and that is the question whether there is in this proposal anything amounting to a breach of contract with judges who have already been appointed to the superior court.
Mr. Speaker, in my view this is a point which it is in a sense difficult to refute but which on a proper analysis of the situation can be refuted completely and specifically. I recognize this is a criticism which was made by Mr. Bennett of the legislation in 1927, although it was disregarded by the government of that day; but that does not seem to me to establish one way or the other the accuracy of the point, merely the fact that it was disregarded.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: Especially as that government changed its mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
It took it three years to do it, and they did it not because they realized the error of their ways; reading of history convinces me that they did it because they were embarrassed over the retirement of a particular judge three years later, but that may be a difference of interpretation too.

The fact of the matter is that there is in my view a fundamental fallacy in this argument that there is a sanctity of contract in this field which is being breached by the legislation now before the house. If hon. members will refer to section 99 of the British North America Act they will find it reads as follows:
The judges of the superior court shall hold office during good behaviour, but shall be removable by the governor general on address of the Senate and House of Commons.
The important thing to bear in mind in reading that section is that there is no mention there that the Senate and House of Commons must assign cause for the removal. I recognize fully that no Senate or House of Commons would act capriciously and simply vote an address to remove a judge from office because it pleased them to do it and it suited their fancy at the moment. It is true they would only act on what to them at that time was represented and accepted as good and sufficient cause. But the fact is that the British North America Act now says that a judge of the superior court can be removed from office by a joint address of the Senate and House of Commons. That is all it says on that point.
That is a provision that has been in the British North America Act since 1867. It is under that provision that every judge appointed to a superior court since 1867 has been appointed, and has been subject to being removed under the provisions of section 99 at any time that the Senate and House of Commons so decide.
What we are submitting to the House of Commons today is that the Senate and House of Commons should decide that the attainment of the age of 75 by a judge of the superior court is sufficient reason to suggest that his office be terminated. That is all that is being suggested. No new legislative principle is being introduced regarding the power of removal from office. All that is happening is that the House of Commons-and the Senate when the address comes up there-will be asked to lay it down as a sound and fundamental rule that with respect to judicial office the attainment of the age of 75 is sufficient reason for the demission of office. That is a right which the Senate and the House of Commons has today and has had since 1867.
On the basis that I have not heard a single member of this house suggest that the general principle of a retirement age at 75 is not sound, it seems to me that all we are asking this house to do is to make that rule of general application instead of leaving it to be applied in any specific case where
Amendment to B.N.A. Act it would have to proved with regard to a particular individual by a terrible and dreadful process, that he had in fact as a result of his attaining the age of 75 become incapacitated in the discharge of his judicial function. I recognize the solidity, if you like, of the point. It is an argument which requires to be dealt with, but in my view it can be dealt with and disposed of completely on that basis alone, as well as on a number of others that I should like to mention.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: Before the minister leaves that point, would he inform me, an unqualified layman on these matters, in view of his argument, what does the expression "good behaviour" mean?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
The expression "good behaviour" has been judicially interpreted on a number of occasions but, with respect to the Leader of the Opposition, that point does not arise in connection with the argument I have been making, since section 99 does not lay down any condition for the passage of an address by the Senate and the House of Commons. It says-and let me read the section again:
The judges of the superior court shall hold office during good behaviour but shall be removable by the governor general on the address of the House of Commons-*

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: Surely one is related to the other.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
I have suggested it was obvious that the Senate and the House of Commons would not act on the basis of caprice or whim, and they are not being asked to do so now. They are being asked to establish that one of the good reasons for the removal of judges from office is the attainment of 75 years, and that is the simple principle before the house.
There are a number of other points I wish to deal with, and I will try to be brief. There is, in addition to the reasons I have advanced, the question of the necessity of uniformity. If we were to accept the argument of the Leader of the Opposition, the result would be that we would have a number of judges appointed prior to this year who could carry on after the age of 75 until they chose to retire or until they died. There would be a number of other judges appointed after this date who would have to retire at the age of 75. Thus there would be a lack of uniformity as between judges with regard to pension rights, retirement rights and terms of office. Apart from the arguments I have advanced on principle, it seems to me that this would be a most undesirable situation, and the undesirability of this situation outweighs in itself any argument advanced by the Leader of the Opposition on the other side.

Amendment to B.N.A. Act

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: Is that not the situation in the United Kingdom now?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
That is the situation in the United Kingdom, but what suits the United Kingdom and what may be applicable there is their responsibility. What is applicable here is our responsibility to determine.
I suggest there is really not much prejudice -if this be one of the grounds of opposition -to the judges who will be affected. As has been pointed out, another resolution now on the order paper will provide for an amendment to the pensions provisions. This amendment will relate the pensions of all judges to the salaries they are now receiving. Whereas at the moment they are related to the salaries in effect before 1955, it will be provided that the judges affected by this measure will have their pension rates adjusted so that they will receive two thirds of the salary they now receive instead of two thirds of the 1955 salaries. It will not be as much, it is true, as though they went out in receipt of their full salaries, but they will retire in receipt of an appreciable advance in comparison with what they would have received had they retired without such provision.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: In principle, the same as the situation in 1933.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
Not at all. Further, we shall be extending to March 1, 1961, by an amendment I shall be moving later, the effective date of this amendment so that there can be no suggestion that judges are being hurried out of office willy-nilly notwithstanding the many years of faithful service they have given.
Finally, I come back to the fact that we have the approval of the provinces. That approval was received on the basis of the letters which I wrote to them and which are recorded in Votes and Proceedings. These letters made no reference to any question of retroactivity with respect to this legislation; I believe I have used the wrong word: they made no reference to the possibility that judges previously appointed would not be affected by this legislation.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: One way or the other.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
One way or the other, and it was not intended that the letters should create that impression. The letters and the discussion I had proceeded on the basis that the legislation would become effective immediately and with respect to all judges whether previously or subsequently appointed. It was on the basis of these letters and that discussion, that provincial consent was received.
In my view, therefore, it would not be open to me to suggest at this stage that I could


consent to an amendment to give effect to the point made by the Leader of the Opposition. Before I could do so I believe I would have to go back to the provinces and ask further consent to what to my mind would be a new proposal rather than the proposal which we have placed before the House of Commons and the Senate.
For all these reasons, while I do not say that the arguments made by the Leader of the Opposition have not got weight-they have, and they must be dealt with, and I have attempted to do so openly and frankly-it is my submission that the interests of the country and the interests of the judiciary are served by imposing a retirement age on the judges of the superior courts and imposing it now so it will be of universal application. As a result, the position of the courts will be uniform throughout the country. The resolution is in the interest of the judiciary and in the interest of the public who go before the courts and are affected by the decisions of the courts; it is in accord with the consents we have received from the provinces and I hope the house will proceed on the basis of the address in its present form subject to the one amendment which I will move later.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT

speechtext: May I be permitted to intervene at this point. maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN

I suggest to the minister that he read his own correspondence with the provinces. The minister will find that with the exception of the government of Quebec in none of the rest of the correspondence is this matter, as I read the correspondence, spelled out in such detail. It is quite true that the hon. gentleman had additional correspondence with the government of Quebec which was not tabled at the time the rest was but I believe it has been made public since.
In any event we know that an address was adopted by the Quebec legislature. We also know that the question of county and district courts is quite irrelevant in the province of Quebec in any case. However, I do not intend to spend very much time on that argument because it is not intrinsically of any importance at all. It is only important as a reflection of the sad state of the minister's mind. What I really think is much more important is the doubt that was raised-and perhaps even more than a doubt in his own case-by the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron) in his reference to the British North America Act 1949, No. 2 which the Prime Minister erroneously referred to this morning as an amendment which gave to this parliament the power to amend the constitution in matters that came within the jurisdiction of this parliament. What it actually does, of course-and I think it is perhaps as well to 79951-0-310
Amendments to B.N.A. Act read the relevant section of it-is to confer upon this parliament the capacity for:
The amendment from time to time of the constitution of Canada, except as regards matters coming within the classes of subjects by this act assigned exclusively to the legislatures of the provinces, or as regards rights or privileges by this or any other constitutional act granted or secured to the legislature of the government of a province-
The rest of it is irrelevant to this debate. That quotation may be found at page 476 of Beauchesne's fourth edition. It is perfectly obvious, in spite of the minister's reference to the administration of justice in section 92, that no one would seriously argue for one moment that the legislature of any province could legislate with respect to the appointment of these judges, either superior court judges or county court judges, or with respect to their tenure; that an attempt on their part to legislate in this particular would be completely beyond their competence because the appointment of these judges at least and the tenure by implication, we argue, in the case of county court judges is given to this parliament; but at any rate the appointment is given to the governor in council and not the provincial governments-

-or as regards rights or privileges by this or any other constitutional act granted or secured to the legislature of the government of a province-
I know many eminent jurists in this country-indeed they are among the most eminent-who take the view that there would be no doubt since that amendment was made in 1949 that parliament could legislate with respect to the tenure of superior court judges. I am rather surprised since the minister emphasized so much the advice of the Canadian Bar Association that he did not take that advice which could have been taken last autumn right after they gave it in September, and make the reference they suggest to the supreme court, because it is perfectly obvious that the eminent members of the Canadian Bar Association who drafted the resolution were of the view that it was at least arguable that it was within the competence of this parliament to legislate in this matter or they would not have suggested a reference to the supreme court.

You know, Mr. Speaker, one is awfully tempted to answer that question but I will resist the temptation. As I was saying when I was interrupted, I do not think that anyone would question that if the British parliament does do what this parliament is going to ask it to do, if the government is successful in getting this motion through in the form in which it wants to put it through, or even in the form in which we are willing to have it go through, I do not think there will be any doubt about the fact that the courts would say that so far as superior courts are concerned it would be valid.
There is some question in my mind, but it is only a question in my mind, and I do not consider I am a sufficiently eminent authority -I do not think perhaps anyone is because in the end it would have to be settled by the court of final resort-but there is some doubt that this parliament, even by a joint address, could confer again upon the British

parliament a jurisdiction of which under the Statute of Westminster it would have appeared to have divested itself. There is no doubt that the British North America Act of 1867 as amended from time to time is the law of Canada and what we usually call the constitution of Canada, but there is nothing in that act which says anything whatever about the tenure of county and district court judges. I question whether in the year 1960 the parliament of Canada by an address can confer upon the British parliament a jurisdiction of which it divested itself when we ceased to be technically a colony in 1931. That it seems to me is a strong additional objection to those made by my leader to the inclusion of county and district courts.
I am going to deal in the opposite order with the arguments of the Minister of Justice and before dealing further with the subject I just mentioned I want to say something about this business of breach of contract. I must say that I thought I had heard the ultimate in casuistry in the past, but I never heard an argument that quite equals the argument put before us today by the Minister of Justice, the suggestion that because this parliament is sovereign it could or would or was designed or intended capriciously to remove judges without cause. The minister went on very quickly to say that we would never do it. I hope we would never do it, but I never thought I would hear any minister of justice get up in this house and say it is a theoretical possibility.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: We can do anything theoretically.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
It is part of a sentence; not a separate sentence, but part of a sentence the other part of which refers to good behaviour which, as the minister has said, is a term of art which has been defined by the courts. What I have understood and what I think most plain-minded people have always understood is that the only way a judge who was guilty of a breach of good behaviour could be removed was by an address of both houses but that this was merely a procedure which could be followed in cases where it was warranted.
Since 1867 we have had life tenure in the superior courts of this country and, as the Prime Minister pointed out this morning- and I do not go about looking for reasons to agree with the Prime Minister but this time I do-the courts of this country are held in as high repute as the courts of any other country, and the judges of this country in as high repute as the judges of any other country, notwithstanding the fact that they have had life tenure for 93 years and, indeed, in

colonial times before that. It does not appear to me that they are suddenly, precipitately, going to deteriorate after March 1, or whatever the date is, 1961, and suddenly become corrupt and incompetent after the age of 75. If we have been able for 93 years to endure the regime that we have now I would think the country would not suffer damage by allowing those judges who have already been appointed to serve out the tenure on which they had accepted their positions from a government and a parliament and a country which on a whole have kept their word.
There is another gentleman with whom I did not often agree in his lifetime but with whom I certainly agree on this occasion. I think that what Mr. Bennett said in 1927 was right, and I am very proud of the fact that Mr. Lapointe came to see that it was right and was a big enough man to change his mind over it. I do not think there is anything to be ashamed of in that at all. But I do think with that precedent it is all the more shocking to ask us to take a course which I can only regard as a dishonourable one.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: The Leader of the Opposition said at the very outset of his remarks that we in this party are in favour of the retirement of judges, appointed after this legislation goes into effect, at the age of 75, but we do not believe we should unilaterally terminate existing contracts. I was astounded to hear the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) suggest that it was quite all right to terminate a contract unilaterally. I can imagine what the hon. gentleman and members of his party would have said if the government had brought in legislation to change unilaterally a collective agreement between labour and management and yet, because those judges are not allowed to enter into collective bargaining, apparently it is quite all right to treat them in a dishonourable fashion, to legislate unilaterally a change in their terms of employment.

speechtext: No, I do not suggest that. I do think that while I would not wish to do it and I would not wish to be a party to it, there would not be very much strength in my argument if the government put forward a proposal even for compulsory retirement on full salary. It then seems to me-

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT

No. I say to the minister I would not wish to be a party to that, but I would think my criticism would be on very much less solid ground if that were done as was done in 1930.	'
Personally I do not think the country would suffer any very great damage from carrying on throughout the lifetime of those judges who do want to stay on after 75-and we know many of them do not, anyway-and are capable of doing it, and if they are not capable of doing it there is machinery now for dealing with them even though the governments have not often used it. They have never used the other machinery of a joint address. Therefore, I say, so far as I am concerned and so far as the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition is concerned, which I am supporting very strongly, I do think that to take this course is to take the course of dishonour.
