On clause 1-Marriage dissolved.

maintopic: EARL BERNARD LAPIERRE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the petition in this particular instance indicates that the petitioner and respondent were married on June 9,	1943, and also that they were
domiciled in Canada, in the province of Quebec, both at the time of the marriage and on the date of this petition. In clause No. 6 of the petition there is an indication that adultery was committed on or about May 6, 1959, and the street address in the city of Montreal is given, as well as the name of the corespondent who is also indicated as living at the same address. Mr. R. A. Cohen appears as counsel for the petitioner.
The petitioner was sworn and gave certain evidence to the clerk of the committee with respect to his name, age, occupation and address. He is asked to give the particulars of the marriage. The first question is;
Q. Are you married?
A. Yes.
Then, he gives the name of his wife and when they were married, which was June 9, 1943, and which date coincides with the date given in the petition. He gives the religious faith to which he belongs, and that of his wife. Then he is shown his marriage certificate. He identifies it and indicates that the statements therein are true. The clerk of the committee states that there were no photographs filed in this particular case and subsequent evidence is given, which I shall relate in a moment, as to how the respondent was identified in this instance.
Then Mr. Cohen asks the petitioner his address, which he gives, and the petitioner indicates he has lived in the city of Montreal for 36 or 37 years which would be almost all of his life. Then Mr. Cohen inquires again about the date of the marriage, as follows:
Q. What year were you married?
A. June 9, 1943.
Q. How long did you live together?
A. About six months.
The next question relates to children and I shall dispense with that because we are forbidden to mention the children here. Then Mr. Cohen says:
Q. Now, after six months of marriage can you tell me why you separated?
A. Well, she was nervous and high strung, and she left a few times, and one time when I came home she was not there, and she never came back.
Q. Did you ever see her over a period of many years?
A. No.
I imagine he means he did not see her for some time, and then there is this question to clarify the situation:
Q. You never saw her since 1943?
A. I have seen her once or twice after that, but it was on the street.

Then he is asked about discussing the question of divorce with his wife, and he says he has not discussed the question of divorce. He indicates also that there is no hope of a reconciliation. The petitioner is asked:
Q. Do you know anything about this-
He gives the name of the corespondent, and the petitioner answers:
A. No, I have never met him. I seen him once on the street, hut I never met him.
The subsequent questions are about when he went to see the lawyer, and so on. Then he is asked some questions about why he went to see the lawyer at that time.
Q. Can you tell us why you came at that time?
A. Well, I received a telephone call from her- well, my sister received a call from her, and I was to call her, and I did not get home until late that night, and I called the next day. That was at her mother's home. She had given that number.
This is, presumably, his wife who phoned, and then Senator Farquhar follows this point up by asking:
Q. What is that you said?
A. Doris called me at my home, and I was not home. I was working. My sister received the call and she told me to call her, but I did not call her that night, and the number to call was her mother's home, ,you see. So I called the next day, and her mother answered the phone.
Then Mr. Cohen wants to know something and asks if he could indicate something about that conversation. He answers:
A. I spoke to her mother, and she said: "You know, Doris does not live here. She is living on Souvenir street"-
Then he gives the name of the corespondent with whom she is living. Subsequently the petitioner went to see his lawyer, and Mr. Cohen asks:
Q. Did you meet anybody there?
A. You introduced me to Mr. Wiseman.
Q. An investigator?
A. Yes.
Q. Where did you go after that?
A. It was May 2. Mr. Wiseman and I went down to Souvenir street, and we waited on the street- I was at your office at about ten, and we waited from about 10.30 until two, and she came out with this man.
Q. Did you point your wife out to Mr. Wiseman?
A. Yes, she walked right up to us, and Mr. Wiseman told me to-
Here, he is interrupted by the chairman, Senator Croll, who asks:
Q. Did you speak to her?
A. Yes, I said: "Hello", and then he took over. He told me to go.
I imagine that was Mr. Wiseman who told him to go.
Q. You spoke to her?
A. I lust said hello to her.
Q. While Wiseman was there?
A. He was right with me, yes.
Q. And-
Then he gives here the name of the corespondent.
Private Bills-Divorce
-was with her?
A. I believe it was-.
And the same name is given.
I am not sure.
Q. Some man was with her?
A. Yes.
Q. There can be no mistake that was your wife? A. Oh, no.
This is the part which substitutes, I imagine, for the photographs, Mr. Chairman, and which was the personal identification, or I would imagine almost an introduction to the investigator, of the respondent. Then Mr. Cohen asks some questions with respect to collusion: By Mr. Cohen:
Q. Did you ever place other men in the way of your wife?
A. No.
Q. And Mr.-
He gives here the name of the corespondent.
-in particular?
A. I never met Mr.-
Giving the corespondent's name.
-outside of that time.
Then Senator Farquhar wants to know why this marriage was discontinued after a six-month period. He asks this question:
Q. What reason did your wife give for leaving you? She must have had a reason.
A. I don't really think so. She was just high-strung and she was very nervous. She was only sixteen years old, I think, and she went home to her mother's place. I know that. I went to a lawyer and sent her a letter and he spoke to her on the phone and she just said she didn't want to live with me.
Then Mr. Cohen asks a question:
Q. How many years ago was that?
A. At the end of 1943.
Senator Gershaw queries further about this matter and asks the following questions:
Q. If she was so high-strung and nervous and only sixteen years old, did you try to console her and try to continue the marriage?
A. I called her back several times, and this lawyer I hired, he called her.
Q. I know, but what I mean is she was young and apparently sick. You said she was nervous and high-strung. Did you get any medical care for her?
A. No, she wasn't that bad that she needed medical care, I don't think. She wasn't that bad. She was just nervous and high-strung.
Then there are questions about work in the house and so on. Then Senator Croll asks how long they had known each other before marriage and the age of the petitioner when he was married and he indicates that he was 21, something like that.
Then Mr. Wiseman appears as a witness on behalf of the petitioner, and here we come to the question of proof of adultery. Mr. Cohen asks Mr. Wiseman questions, the first of which was as follows:
Q. Mr. Wiseman, I don't have a photograph to show you, but could you tell this committee when you saw the respondent-

Private Bills-Divorce
He gives there the name of the respondent.
-for the first time.
A. She was pointed out to me by her husband on May 2, 1959.
Q. Where, sir?
A. By her place of domicile,-
He gives there the address which is the same as the address indicated in the petition as being that where adultery had taken place and also of the residence of the respondent and the corespondent. I might say that this is an instance of a common law arrangement. These two people had been living together for a number of years. Evidence to that effect was given later on. Mr. Wiseman is asked additional questions by Mr. Cohen about this particular meeting when the wife was pointed out to him:
Q. Could you tell us something about that meeting? How was she pointed out?
A. Mr.-
And he gives there the name of the petitioner.
-went with me simply because we didn't have a photograph. To make positive identification I requested he come with me, and he pointed his wife out to me when she came out of the building.
Q. Was there anybody else present?
A. The corespondent.
Q. You had never seen this man before that?
A. No.
Then there are questions again about the particular investigation. Mr. Wiseman answers by saying as follows:
A. Between May 2nd and May 6th, 1959, I conducted an investigation very discreetly, asking several people questions in the neighbourhood and I learned that the respondent was living with Mr. 
*
He gives here the name of the corespondent.
-as man and wife and was known as Mrs.-
He gives here the surname of the corespondent.
-at that address. On May 6th, 1959, my associate, Mr. O'Neil and myself proceeded to the domicile of the respondent, arriving shortly after 11 o'clock. We rang the bell of the domicile of the respondent and it was answered by her. We asked for Mrs.-
He gives here the married name of the respondent.
-and she first said "There is no Mrs.-"
He gives here that same name.
She was very sketchy about it. She said "I am Mrs.-.
And he gives here the surname of the corespondent.
-and I said "Aren't you known as Mrs.-?"
And he gives here her true name or married name.
-and at the same time I identified myself to her when I said that, and she said "Yes, I am Mrs.-"
And he gives here her correct name.
-and she asked me to come in. We went into the flat and the corespondent-

And he gives here the name.
-was in there. They had evidently been watching television. The television set was on. I can remember quite well because the news was on at the time we arrived.
Q. What time was that?
A. Between 11 and 11.15.
Q. Could you describe to this committee Mrs.-?
And there is given here the name of the respondent.
A. I would say she is a woman in her early thirties, about five foot four, five foot five, with jet black hair, medium build, about 110 or 115.
Q. How did Mr.-
And here there is given the name of the corespondent.
-look?
A. Mr.- is a man in his mid or early thirties, quite tall, five foot eleven or six foot, fairly heavily built.
Q. Did you have any conversation with her?
A. Yes. As a matter of fact, they were most co-operative when they learned I was there, although she was a little surprised that Mr.-
And here there is given the name of the petitioner.
-was taking this action after a separation of over ten years. She seemed to be quite happy and they invited us in and we must have spent every bit of a half hour in the place. They were talkative people and he went on to explain that he was a chemist employed at C.I.L. and he was working on some photographic formula at the time for coloured picture for a Polaroid camera, for instant colour shots.
Q. Were there any other people there?
A. No.
Q. Could you describe the house?
A. Yes, it is what I would call a five-room flat with a bedroom, living room-dining room combination and there was an archway and there was what I would call a utility room with a washer, a dryer and a deep freeze in there. It was all very orderly.
Q. Did they admit living there together as mar and wife?
A. Oh, yes, and that they had been for quite a number of years.
Q. How long did you wait after you left the premises?
A. We were in the house for half an hour when they admitted being together, and through my prior investigation having learned they were living together as man and wife I didn't see any reason to wait when I came out. They were both dressed for bed, in pyjamas, just as any ordinary married couple would be or if I was spending the evening at home with my wife I would have been spending the evening just about in the same way.
Mr. Ronald O'Neil is called to give evidence. He was the partner of Mr. Wiseman. He is questioned by Mr. Cohen as follows:
Q. I don't have a photograph to show you, but could you describe to this committee if you ever saw a-?
A. -yes.
Q. Where did you see her?
A,-near Cannon street, Montreal.
Q. About what time?
A. 11.15, 11.10 p.m. on May 6, 1959.
Q. Could you describe to this committee what Mrs.-looked like?
A. She was about five five, five six, maybe 115 pounds.

Q. Approximate age?
A. Thirty two, thirty three, something like that, in that area.
Q. Did you go into this residence at-?
A. Yes. I did.
Q. Could you tell us what happened when you were inside?
A. A Mr. Wiseman and myself entered the premises and Mrs.-is the one who answered the door-that is the name she gave us when she answered the door, and Mr. Wiseman said "Are you Mrs.-?" and she said that she was Mrs.- and Mr. Wiseman said, "Aren't you Mrs.-?" and she said yes, and she invited us in and Mr. Wiseman told her what we were there for and she said "I don't understand it after so many years"-they had been separated ten years-"why he is doing that now?" We said "We don't know."
Q. Was there anybody else in the house?
A. Yes,-
Q. What did he look like?
A. He was a man of about thirty six, thirty seven, maybe six foot tall, 180, 190 pounds, somewhere in that area.
Q. Was there any conversation that went on that evening when you were in the apartment with Mrs.-, Mr. Wiseman, Mr.-and yourself?
A. Yes. Mr.-told us a bit of his history and what he was doing, and asked us how divorce worked and he thought there had to be pictures taken and he said he was working for C.I.L. colour pictures, and the conversation was regarding that kind of stuff.
Q. How were they dressed?
A. He was wearing apair of bluish-gray pyjamas.
Q. And Mrs.-?
A. She had on a pair of pink pyjamas with a house-coat or robe down to her knees.
Q. Did they admit in front of you that they were living as man and wife?
A. Yes, they had for several years.
By Senator Gershaw:
Q. From the general appearance of the place were you convinced that they had been living there as man and wife for some time?
A. Yes, I would say so. There was one bedroom with women's and men's clothes hanging in the clothes closet; there was only one bed in the house, a large double bed.
Q. A three quarters or double bed?
A. I don't think I would be able to recognize the difference.
Mr. Chairman, it is necessary to indicate all that for this reason. The petition says that on or about May 6, 1959, at a particular address adultery was committed. The preamble to the bill, which we have not read yet, indicates that the marriage was on such and such a date and that adultery had been proved by evidence adduced, and so on. I submit that it is jumping to conclusions to say that adultery took place on that particular day. If the basis of a common law arrangement is such that this could be ground for divorce perhaps there might be some validity to the suggestion that adultery had been proved.
According to the evidence, at no time during the half hour that these two investigators were on the premises talking with the respondent and corespondent did they get around to talking about adultery. They talked about Polaroid cameras and photographic formulas, about why he would want to take
Private Bills-Divorce
action to get a divorce, and I presume they talked about a number of other things too. Presumably they went through the premises and got a good look at them because they give evidence of the number of rooms there, what was in them, such as a washer, dryer, deep-freeze, that there were clothes in the closets, and so on.
In my opinion all that has been proved is that this couple lived together as man and wife under a common law arrangement. From what we have been able to gather as to what is adultery, even though we are not allowed apparently to speculate about what the word means, that is not the case in this particular instance. That is why I went extensively into the evidence, to show that all that had been proved was that this couple were in their pyjamas and were spending the evening somewhat in the same manner as Mr. Wiseman would spend the evening with his wife if he were not out investigating divorce cases, and that they sat and talked for half an hour. While they admitted that they had been living together as man and wife and that there was a common law arrangement, I submit that that is the basis upon which we should consider granting this divorce, not on the basis of adultery having taken place, because according to the evidence given by Mr. Wiseman and Mr. O'Neil there is not a word about adultery. We do not know whether they discussed it in the half an hour they were there or whether they attempted to discover whether adultery had taken place between this particular couple on that particular day.
Mr. Chairman, I submit there is not one shred of evidence to indicate that adultery did take place. It may well have after the detectives left. This is a possibility if they were living together as man and wife but I submit that this is the basis upon which we should consider granting a divorce, their living together as common law man and wife, and not on the basis of adultery having been proved.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: EARL BERNARD LAPIERRE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in this particular case, as in a number of other cases, we have the odd situation where a couple were married many years ago. They broke up in 1943. At that time the girl was 16, her husband was 21 or in that neighbourhood, and they lived apart with no particular attempt to dissolve the marriage for 16 years. They now come before us asking for dissolution of marriage and charging that adultery has taken place.
It has not been proved that this is the gentleman. If the case is to be accepted at face value it is not indicated whether this was the alliance that this young lady set up

Private Bills-Divorce
in 1943. In any case, from reading the evidence it is clearly indicated that no attempt made on the part of the husband during these years from 1943 to 1959 to do something about this situation and either relieve himself of an unwanted wife or the wife seek relief from a husband with whom she had no contact. On page 12 of the evidence appear the following questions:
Q. Did you ever see her over a period of many years?
A. No.
Q. You never saw her since 1943?
A. I have seen her once or twice after that but it was on the street.
Under English law, one of the discretionary bars is this matter of delay and it would seem to me that in this particular instance we have not got the whole story about what happened. It would seem to me that the husband would have been more interested at the time in retaining his wife. As a husband he would have been interested in keeping his wife with him. I am not too impressed about the evidence he gave as to her keeping house. He seemed sketchy about whether she kept house or not but he finally admitted she did. There must have been some loss about her leaving home.
Kent Power points out that discretionary bars are not absolute in the prevention of divorce but they are a large factor. He has this to say on page 82:
The delay which under the act of 1857 is a discretionary bar is "unreasonable delay" in presenting or prosecuting the petition. The same discretion exists in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia.
The reason these two provinces are mentioned is that both follow the original British law.
The delay of the respondent in putting in a defence is a factor to be considered in deciding whether cross-relief asked for therein should be granted. The reason for the court frowning on delay was thus expressed by Sir Francis Jeune in Johnson v. Johnson-

maintopic: EARL BERNARD LAPIERRE
speechtext: We cannot allow this to go on. The hon. member is reading about a respondent's rights, the rights of respondents instead of the rights of petitioners. He has neglected the evidence on page 12 which clearly shows that the husband was not aware he had recourse to parliament until April, 1959. It is a typical type of debating such as we have heard for months and months; the reading of some evidence and then the picking up of a law book to try to get a paragraph to throw into the pot as well. I submit that what the hon. member is reading is completely irrelevant. It has nothing to do with the facts. If the hon. member would follow the argument as to how the husband found he had a cause of action he will find he is out of order.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: EARL BERNARD LAPIERRE
speechtext:
English law says that the
defence or prosecution of the case must take place within a reasonable length of time, and I suggest that by no stretch of the imagination can 16 years be considered a reasonable length of time. A contract of marriage carries with it certain obligations and privileges and when those privileges are withdrawn the plaintiff has the right if he does not condone or connive, to take discretionary action as soon as possible. Sixteen years in this case constitutes in my opinion an unreasonable amount of delay. I should like to refer to what has been said in connection with other legal decisions which have been made by the courts on this question.

maintopic: EARL BERNARD LAPIERRE
speechtext: If I may again refer to the point of order, may I point out that the cause of action was not discovered by the husband in 1943; it was discovered in April 1959. When he had a cause of action he pursued it forthwith, so this argument based on the marriage breaking up after 17 years is not relevant. The woman might have been anywhere during that time, living as a single person, by herself. We are getting into an irrelevant line of legal discussion. No matter how the hon. member tries to twist or interpret facts there is still sworn evidence, and it is the only evidence we have on this point.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: EARL BERNARD LAPIERRE
speechtext: If I may just continue the discussion on this aspect, I suggest that the fact that 16 years had gone by before an application was made is only an indication that the plaintiff in this particular case had made a liaison or a connection; he had found a girl friend, and therefore he was ready to pursue this-

maintopic: EARL BERNARD LAPIERRE
speechtext: I rise on a question of privilege. I do not think any member of the House of Commons has the right to get up on his feet and make an allegation against a member of the general public who is not here to defend himself, without a jot or tittle of evidence to back it up. I think it is unjust and a corruption of the processes of the house for any hon. member to come in and abuse someone without one single solitary fact of evidence to support the allegation.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: EARL BERNARD LAPIERRE
speechtext: Of course, the hon. member has taken the responsibility for the statements he makes in this house. I can only say that for his guidance.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: EARL BERNARD LAPIERRE
speechtext: In discussing this matter of unreasonable delay I do so because I think it has some bearing on this case. I think this should answer the hon. member for Halifax who is concerned, or should be concerned, with this particular matter.

maintopic: EARL BERNARD LAPIERRE
speechtext: So should you.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: EARL BERNARD LAPIERRE
speechtext:
I am. I quote again:
The reasons why this court insists on steps being taken promptly, if they are to be taken at all, and why it should be very strenuous on the subject of delay, are that it is a terrible thing that people should be going about the world neither married nor unmarried, possibly liable to contract fresh and illegal matrimony and certainly exposed to temptation to commit adultery. That is a state of things which ought not to be prolonged for a moment longer than it can properly be avoided.
It goes on:
Referring to the argument that the stringent rules of earlier decisions had been relaxed, McLaurin said-

maintopic: EARL BERNARD LAPIERRE
speechtext: Again I rise on a point of order. The point I have been trying to make, with success I imagine with everyone except the hon. member, is that if there was any evidence of any delay in bringing this case before parliament then the hon. member's reading would be relevant, but all the evidence we have on record here indicates that the man found his wife was living with somebody else in April, 1959. Apparently he did not know what she had been doing in the interim. That being so, he proceeded with due haste to present himself to parliament, and this talk about delay is, I submit, entirely irrelevant unless the hon. member can point to one jot of evidence which would help support his contention.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: EARL BERNARD LAPIERRE
speechtext: Of course, the rule of relevancy applies when we discuss this kind of bill just as when we are discussing any other kind of bill, but I must say I can hardly decide that an argument which would appear to be unfounded, as explained by the hon. member who rises on the point of order, is irrelevant. I cannot assess the value of the arguments that are brought forward by hon. members who have the floor. What the hon. member for Halifax says may be so. I think it would then be a matter for the hon. member for Halifax to answer when he has the floor.

After all, he was only 21 when the marriage broke up. I imagine they were not too grown up. Although these parties lived together for a time the divorce is sought not on the grounds of the alliance as a relief to the community and the end of an intolerable situation but on the grounds of adultery.
I doubt if many hon. members of this committee or the other place have satisfied themselves as to what constitutes adultery in legal terms. I will read the evidence which purports to show that adultery occurred. On page 14 Mr. C. Wiseman, a Montreal investigator who has figured in other cases was questioned by Mr. Cohen as follows:
Q. Could you tell us what happened with your investigation thereafter?
A. Between May 2nd and May 6th, 1959, X conducted an investigation very discreetly, asking several people questions in the neighbourhood and
I	learned that the respondent was living with Mr. Patterson as man and wife and was known as Mrs. Patterson at that address. On May 6th, 1959, my associate, Mr. O'Neil and myself proceeded to the domicile of the respondent, arriving shortly after
II	o'clock. We rang the bell of the domicile of the respondent and it was answered by her. We asked for Mrs. Lapierre and she first said "There is no Mrs. Lapierre". She was very sketchy about it. She said, "I am Mrs. Patterson" and I said "Aren't you known as Mrs. Lapierre?" and at the same time I identified myself to her when I said that, and she said "Yes, I am Mrs. Lapierre" and she asked me to come in. We went into the flat and the corespondent, Arthur Patterson, was in there. They had evidently been watching television. The television set was on. I can remember quite well because the news was on at the time we arrived.
In my opinion this is sufficient evidence to establish a common law alliance and yet it is not indicated that adultery had been committed. I would point out that before long this committee is going to be asked to rule on a number of cases where people did live together as man and wife for some time. We are being asked to grant an annulment when no cohabitation by these people has been established in the sense that marriage was consummated. I am suggesting that this type of common law evidence, while I think it is sufficient in my mind to grant the divorce, does not constitute adultery and
[Mr. Peters-l
adultery is one of the grounds that is mentioned in the petition before us today.
They go on to discuss the case; they talk about the things that were discussed. The corespondent and the respondent in this case were very cordial people. They discussed photography. I agree that this always interests me. The corespondent was of the impression that pictures should be taken in this type of situation; that pictures were necessary. He was surprised that they were not necessary. He was enlightened by the investigators who informed him what the procedure was.
This is a case where they did not break down the door. The atmosphere seemed to be fairly friendly and quite informal. There is nothing in the evidence to indicate to me and I think to any hon. member that adultery in the true sense of the word was committed on this particular date. The questioning continued:
Q. Could you describe the house?
A. Yes, it was what I would call a 5-room flat with a bedroom, living room-dining room combination and there was an archway and there was what I would call a utility room with a washer, a dryer and a deep freeze in there. It was all very orderly.
It was all very orderly but the previous husband indicated the housekeeping was something that one could not be too proud about in so far as the previous marriage was concerned, but this is only an incidental thing. Q. Did they admit living together as man and wife?

We were in the house for half an hour when they admitted being together, and through my prior investigation having learned they were living together as man and wife I didn't see any reason to wait when I came out. This again is an indication that a common law alliance had been set up, but I ask hon. members, would they not have to stretch their imaginations considerably to establish an adultery charge on those grounds? I would imagine that we would see people wandering around in this condition or a condition very similar to it-maybe the clothing would be a little more expensive-at most of the summer resorts where people sit around with not too much on, usually shorts and a halter and the men wearing shorts and swimming

trunks, or whatever they are, that they sit around in. At the ski lodges they sit around with very little more on than this watching television. The apparel may be a little more costly because it is considered to be casual toggery, lounging wear instead of sleeping wear. There is very little difference in this case. I am in complete agreement that the divorce could be granted in this case on other grounds and probably should be, but there has been no admission that adultery took place on this particular day.
I should like to draw your attention to the fact, Mr. Chairman, that they did not even wait to see whether these people remained there overnight. At no time did they stay or observe the house during the period that they normally stay around and watch places. They did not wait until 2.30 in the morning to see whether the people came out or to collect a few extra bucks. They did not wait because they found the people were both dressed for bed. speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Diefenbaker for an address to Her Majesty the Queen praying that a measure be laid before the parliament of the United Kingdom to amend the British North America Act, 1867, relating to the amendment of the constitution of Canada, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Pearson.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the business of the house was interrupted at five o'clock I had, I think, rather thoroughly disposed of the shabby, casuistical arguments of the Minister of Justice, that in breaking a contract he was not breaking a contract because this was a sovereign parliament that could do anything anyway. This is the kind of argument that I hardly expected to hear from the Minister of Justice in a government that is proposing, later in this session, to introduce

Amendment to B.N.A. Act a bill of rights. I do not believe I need to labour that argument any longer, because I think it is equally important that I should deal with the two other arguments that the Minister of Justice made.
He seemed to argue that there was something unsatisfactory about the status and tenure of county and district court judges at the present time; that they did not have a security of tenure equal to that of high court judges. Of course, that is true, and it is well understood. There have been a good many cases I believe since confederation when county and district court judges have been removed by the procedure that is provided. I speak subject to correction, but I know of no case in which there has been an address of the two houses of parliament to remove a high court judge. In effect, what we will be asking the parliament at Westminster to do, if we pass this address in the form in which the government is asking to have it passed, is to make the county court judges virtually as irremovable as high court judges are now. I do not feel competent to discuss the question-

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
-of whether or not county court judges and high court judges should have the same tenure and the same status. I am not, and if the good wishes I see manifest in some parts of the house are any indication, there are many people who think I am never likely to be a member of the bar, and I am rather inclined to agree that is unlikely. Many of my learned friends on this side of the house are much more competent than I would ever be to discuss this question, and will discuss it.
In so far as the constitutional point is concerned, I do have some observations to make. My view is that if the tenure of county court judges should be assimilated to the tenure of high court judges, that would be a competent thing for this parliament to do. I must say I am quite unimpressed by the arguments of the Minister of Justice that in these latter days he has suddenly discovered that all his precedessors throughout history were wrong; that Sir John Macdonald was wrong when he thought this parliament was competent to legislate with respect to the tenure of county court judges; that Sir Charles Fitzpatrick was wrong when in 1903 he introduced a limitation on the age of county court judges; that Mr. Doherty was wrong when in 1913 he asked parliament, and parliament acceded, to reduce the age to 75 years. It does seem extraordinary, when one comes to think about some of the people who have occupied the position the minister now occupies that they could all have been wrong.


There was Sir John Macdonald, Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, Mr. Edward Blake. There were ministers like Mr. Lapointe, Mr. St. Laurent and great legal luminaries like Mr. Bennett. It seems extraordinary that all these great lawyers of the past should have been mistaken in the view that parliament had undoubted jurisdiction, and that suddenly a great light dawned upon the hon. member for Kamloops when he became minister and he discovered that what had been done without any question up to this time had some constitutional doubt about it.
In my opinion, this is a preposterous suggestion. Like some other members of the house, I have known a few county court judges who have retired at the age of 75 rather unwillingly. Some of them were quite good lawyers and, if it is not disrespectful to say of a retired judge, some of them were rather cantankerous people, too. I would guess that if any of these gentlemen had suspected there was any constitutional flaw in the legislation by which they were retired they would have taken the case into court. If the minister did have a doubt, and I cannot believe that the minister is so self-assured about this matter as to think that where all the ministers of justice in the past were wrong he is right, we have a constitutional procedure for resolving these doubts. I refer to the procedure which was suggested by the bar association in the resolution which the minister himself read to us, the resolution that was adopted last September. It does seem to me very difficult to comprehend the course being followed.
The Canadian Bar Association did suggest to the government the course to take in dealing with this matter. After all, the bar association did not call into question the status of county court judges or district court judges; they only raised the question with respect to superior court judges. They suggested that at least there was an argument. Otherwise they would never have s.uggested, I submit, a reference to the supreme court. They suggested that at least there was an argument that it was competent for this parliament, under the terms of the second amendment of 1949 to the British North America Act, to legislate with respect to the tenure of superior court judges.
As I say, a reference to the court could have been made last September and by this time this parliament could have had the opinion of the supreme court as to whether it would be competent, as the bar association apparently thought it might be, to do it in this way. But the government has chosen to do it in the other way. As the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) has indicated, we do not quarrel with that procedure with

Amendment to B.N.A. Act
respect to superior court judges who may be appointed after the coming into force of this legislation, if the amendment of the Leader of the Opposition is accepted and if the address passes in the amended form, as we would be quite satisfied to have it pass. We feel that there will be no reasonable doubt if this is done, that it will be a valid amendment to the constitution and that it will be respected by the courts in so far as the superior court judges are concerned.
But with respect to county court judges there does not seem to us to be any kind of argument that can seriously be considered. I said earlier that I could not really believe that anyone would argue that a provincial legislature could validly legislate to determine the tenure of county court judges or superior court judges. I would certainly think that a provincial legislature could not legislate with respect to superior court judges as long as the British North America Act contains the present provision. But I suppose an argument could be made that in the constitution of the courts it might be possible for the provinces to limit the tenure of county court judges. But I repeat that it is surprising that such an argument never seems to have occurred to Sir John Macdonald or Sir Charles Fitzpatrick or to Mr. Charles Doherty, all of whom dealt with this matter and none of whom ever called into question the jurisdiction of this parliament over this matter.
In view of the fact that outside of the Minister of Justice nobody else seems to have had any doubts about this matter, I hope that the government, if it feels that this matter needs to be resolved, will do it by accepting the amendment offered by the Leader of the Opposition and will refer this question to the courts, if they feel a reference is needed. I myself confess that I do not feel that it is needed; I do not think there is any doubt that is worth considering. However, if they feel there is a doubt, I hope they will refer the matter to the courts. Surely it is the height of colonialism-and no other word can be applied to it-to seek to vest in Westminster a jurisdiction which they have never had- which they did not assume in 1867 and of which certainly, once the Statute of Westminster was passed, they divested themselves -and to seek to put into a British statute something no one has ever questioned since 1867 until the minister had this bright idea quite recently, namely the right of this parliament to do something which this parliament has done over and over again and which has been the basis of the tenure of county and district court judges since the year 1913 without any kind of question. It almost passes comprehension why a government should seek to be so abject.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman can make a speech in his own time and refute the argument and give any good reason at all why this should be done. As I said at the beginning of my remarks, I think there is some real question whether by an address of two houses of this parliament, we can properly and constitutionally vest once more in the parliament of Westminster something of which it divested itself at the time of the Statute of Westminster. This is not an amendment to the British North America Act at all. This is not an amendment at all. This is putting into the British North America Act something that has never been there. In so far as county and district courts are concerned, it is a new enactment. As far as superior court judges are concerned, I quite grant that it is an amendment and quite a valid one. Our only objection to that amendment-and, as I said before the dinner recess, it is a matter about which we feel strongly-is this breach of contract which we think is totally unnecessary in view of the fact that we have had this regime for 93 years and, as the Prime Minister said in his opening speech, the courts of this country and the judges of this country will compare favourably with those of any other country.

Will the hon. gentleman indicate why he thinks the attorney general of Newfoundland agreed to this proposal in the light of the strictures which the hon. gentleman has been uttering?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: I am not the keeper of any other man's conscience. I speak for myself in this house and I will go on doing so. If I disagree with any man, however eminent he may be, whether he is the attorney general of any province, the Minister of Justice, the Prime Minister or anyone else and if I think I have a sound view, in a free country and in a free parliament I will express those views. The hon. gentleman does not need to think that he embarrasses me in the slightest by asking a question of that sort. In the first place, of course, that letter from the attorney general of Newfoundland which the Prime Minister read earlier today and which I will not read into the record again merely says that they are quite agreeable to this amendment. But in the language of any of those letters, except the correspondence with the government of Quebec, there is nothing that indicates anything pro or con their feeling on the question of retroactive legislation.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: What is your stand?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman knows perfectly well what my stand is. I stand for honouring contracts, not for breaking them. That is our view. I am sure the attorney general of any province receiving that letter from the minister would have thought that obviously the minister was not going to break contracts but that what he was going to do was to ask for legislation regarding the tenure of appointments to be made from now on and not to change the terms of employment, the terms of a contract between Her Majesty and the judges of this country; and that is what the government in this address is seeking to do.
The worst feature of it all is that we are content to dishonour ourselves in this parliament. We are asking the British parliament to pass an act breaking contracts in this country. We are asking the British parliament to say that the tenure of office and remuneration of judges which they accepted and the terms of their employment should be changed by a statute of another country than their own. It seems to me that this is a shocking disrespect for the parliament of another country, to ask them to rubber stamp legislation which is so manifestly unjust, as this would be, as applied to the present incumbents.
I want to make it very clear again that so far as any appointments that may be made, if this legislation goes through, after the passing of this act are concerned, we are entirely in favour of the 75 years retirement age for anyone who accepts his employment on that basis. We think that is quite

right and proper, as far as I am concerned for the reasons the Prime Minister gave at the beginning of the discussion. But we think that it is equally wrong to make these unilateral changes, and we think it would be wrong in the case, above all, of the judges whose position and independence should be safeguarded above that of anybody else in the community.
I return again to this other totally unnecessary, totally uncalled for and totally hypothetical proposal with respect to county and district court judges. It really is quite impossible to comprehend why the government should want to do this. What do they think they are going to accomplish by doing it?
