speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the main purpose for which I rise now is to move the amendment to which the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) referred this afternoon but before doing so there are one or two other things which I think should be said. In my remarks this afternoon I attempted to keep the discussion on a factual and non-political level but in the remarks that he made during the course of the afternoon and so far this evening the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) did his best to remove the discussion from that sphere and take it into the sphere of Alice in Wonderland-to use a phrase the hon. member himself used.
Rumour has it that the hon. member foi Bonavista-Twillingate stayed up all last evening to prepare his address for today and I must say that after listening to him I can well believe that is a fact because his remarks did seem to lie more in the realm of dreamland and fantasy than in a realm in which his remarks could have any relationship or bearing on the facts of the situation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: Just a plain nightmare.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
My friend the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) says, "Just a plain nightmare" but I think the remarks of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate were perhaps not nightmare so much as fantasy because fantasy, as I understand it, is a matter that has no relationship to reality, whereas nightmare is sometimes founded on reality.
The reality of this situation is that the government asks parliament to consent to an address to Her Majesty to bring in a provision that judges of the superior courts will retire at the age of 75. In this respect the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, in so far as he addressed himself to the proposition before the house, dealt with two subjects: First, the question of whether or not there is here a breach of contract; and, second, whether or not there is a retrograde step in placing the position of district and county court judges under the constitution.
I have seldom heard so distorted an argument as that made by the hon. gentleman to the effect that to seek to place the position of judges of district and county courts of

Amendement to B.N.A. Act Canada under the constitution is a retrograde step. Yet that was the argument made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: Not at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: In an attempt to bolster his political position the hon. gentleman used charges of colonialism and similar inept words. Of course if we were to follow the course of my hon. friends opposite and the government that preceded us of which the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was a member there might be some foundation for that charge but as I said this afternoon it is our intention-and we believe it will be successful-that the constitution of Canada will be repatriated. That is unlike the history of this matter under our predecessors when I recall the minister of justice of those days riding into battle dressed in shining armour as the great emancipator, the one who was to free the constitution of the slavery in which it was then enthralled and whose efforts of course fell to the ground. From there on it seemed quite acceptable to hon. gentlemen opposite including, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, that they should rest there.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: What have you done?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
If, therefore, we were to be content with that position there might be some foundation for the hon. member's charge. But as it is, his charge rests on no surer foundation than a suggestion that it is improper to regulate the relationships between parliament, the executive and an important branch of the judiciary by reference to the constitution.
Of course, as I recall some of the things that were done by the former government I can well understand their resentment of the attempt now being made to place the position of the judiciary with respect to the county and district courts on the sure basis of the constitution-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: Of the British parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: My friend the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and the Leader of the Opposition by his endorsement of that argument would prefer to have the judiciary-the county court judges particularly-left to have their tenure of office-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: In Canadian hands.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: -determined-

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: By the parliament of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
-by the government with no reference to the constitution whatever.

To show how inept and inapplicable all these arguments are may I refer to a case of 1930 which dealt with the question of whether or not there is a breach of contract involved in the address which is before the house. I believe this is the only serious point that has been made by my hon. friends opposite. I attempted to deal with it on a factual basis this afternoon but nothing of factual argument appears to impress my hon. friends opposite so perhaps I might reinforce my argument by a reference to judgments of the Supreme Court of Canada and of the privy council which dealt with that case.
I must refer to the stand taken both by the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate when they charged us with introducing through this address a form of breach of contract. It was interesting, Mr. Speaker, as Your Honour will recall, shortly before five o'clock to find the seriousness with which my hon. friends held to that view. You remember the vigour with which they made the charge that this represents a breach of contract. But I am sure you will remember also the answer of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate to two or three questions that were asked him in that regard when it became apparent that all he was concerned about was not principle but price, and the only thing-

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, the minister has said something which he knows is completely untrue. The truth is I said I would not wish to be a party to this kind of proposition at all, but that my argument would not be as strong if the persons who are to be retired did not suffer at all financially. I said I would not be a party to it at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the sensitivity of the hon. gentleman. Just how he distinguishes between an argument which is strong and an argument which is less strong when neither of them rests on any secure foundation at all I am unable to say. The fact of the matter is that my hon. friend in effect agreed that the main difference between us was the extent to which-

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: No, I did not agree.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
-the judges who would be affected by this resolution might lose some monetary interest that they had in their present position.
Well, sir, that is a concern that I can understand, and I attempted to deal with it on a factual basis this afternoon by pointing out that they would not really suffer any

great disadvantage in that the effective date of the change had been postponed to March 1 and in the interim we were bringing in substantial changes to the pension provision. Notwithstanding that argument, notwithstanding that my hon. friend had to agree that the real difference between us was price and not principle, he went on to repeat that there was here a breach of contract. Let me refer him to a case which arose as the result of certain actions taken by the government of Mr. Mackenzie King in 1930, as they affected the case of a Mr. Reilly. I think it was in 1923 that Mr. Clifford B. Reilly had been appointed a member of a commission dealing with pensions. The case of Clifford B. Reilly and His Majesty the King is reported in the Supreme Court of Canada Reports, 1932, and the case before the privy council is reported in the Law Reports, Appeal Cases, 1934.
Mr. Reilly had been appointed by order in council and by commission as a member of the federal appeal board under section 10 of an act to amend the Pension Act, 1923. His appointment was extended on a number of occasions, the last extension being for a period of five years from August 17, 1928. Now, notwithstanding the high regard which my hon. friends opposite had for this principle of sanctity of contract, notwithstanding that they had appointed a man and then extended his appointment at, he alleged, great personal sacrifice on assuming the office and on retaining it-they extended his appointment for a period of five years from August 17, 1328-my hon. friends opposite or their predecessors by solemn legislative enactment abolished the office as one of their last acts as a government on May 30, 1930. Mr. Reilly accordingly sued the crown, claiming damages for breach of contract-

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: Shame.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
The Supreme Court of Canada in a judgment delivered by Mr. Justice Orde, judge ad hoc, gave the following judgment:
Here there was no dismissal from office by the crown in the ordinary sense. Parliament abolished the office. The power of the crown to abolish a civil office and thereby to deprive the holder thereof of any right to further compensation is recognized in Young v. Waller. If in cases where its power is not restricted by statute the crown may abolish an office, a fortiori parliament which created it must surely possess the power.
This is a judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada, and I always understood, in spite of what he said this afternoon that my hon. friend, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate, does have, when it consorts with his argument, a due regard for the courts of the
Amendment to B.N.A. Act land. Then I would hope that he would recognize that in this case the Supreme Court of Canada has itself established the basis of the refutation of his argument, his absurd argument, his nightmarish, fantastic argument, his Alice in Wonderland argument, that there is here a breach of contract-

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: Will the minister permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
-for the parliament under
whose authority a man was appointed to office-

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: Will the minister permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: Will the minister tell us whether the office that Mr. Reilly held was an office consecrated under the British North America Act guaranteeing tenure for life during good behaviour? If not, of course the case does not apply at all.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: Is that part of the question?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: It is quite obvious that even if I read the whole of the judgment my hon. friend would not agree with it, and therefore I am not going to read the judgment because the question is answered by what I have already said and quoted from the judgment.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: It has no bearing whatever.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member may be more impressed by the judgment of the privy council. As I say, Mr. Reilly appealed the case to the privy council. The judgment was given in the privy council by Lord Atkin, as reported at page 176 and 177 and following pages in Appeal Cases, 1934. Lord Atkin had this to say, among other things, with respect to the question of contract. You see, Mr. Speaker, what my hon. friends fail to realize is that they have based their case on the argument that there was a contract between the government and the judges who are appointed, and in so far as that is their allegation, then this case and this judgment are exactly in point. If my hon. friends would come to the heart of the matter and recognize that there is no contract then, of course, the situation might be different. I am taking it on their basis.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: What did Mr. Bennett say about it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
If I have to get into Alice in Wonderland a little bit I apologize, but I have

Amendment to B.N.A. Act to follow the arguments that have been made. Lord Atkin said as follows:
So far as the rights and obligations rested on contract, further performance of the contract had been made by statute impossible, and the contract was discharged.
Then this is an interesting part of the judgment:
It is perhaps unnecessary to add that discharged means put an end to and does not mean broken. In the result, therefore, the appellant has failed to show a breach of contract on which to found damages.
Then Lord Atkin goes on a little later:
Finally, and almost inevitably in such a case, an appeal was made to the British North America Act, and it was said that legislation abolishing the office without compensation was an interference with "property and civil rights". But, as before, if the right was in itself determinable by statute, there was no interference with it.
Then he continues:
It would be strange that the dominion should have power to create an office but no power to abolish it except on the terms of awarding compensation apparently for the full term of the original office.
This is exactly what the hon. member is asking us to do.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: Will the minister permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: Not for just a moment. They have agreed there is no difference in principle but only in price, and what they say is-

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: That is not true.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
What they are saying in effect is because you are terminating the services you can only do it on the basis that you have to continue the salary.
My hon. friend has said his argument would not be nearly as strong if we were prepared to allow those judges to continue at the same salary even although they ceased to serve as judges which is, to my mind, an entirely untenable position. I come back to the point made by Lord Atkin that it would be strange that an authority or authorities having the power to create an office have no power to terminate it except on the condition that they should continue to pay compensation, measured by the full salary that the incumbents were receiving before the office was terminated.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: Will the minister now permit my question?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
My question is this: Is the minister contending that the dominion, in the sense Lord Atkin used it, created the office of superior court judge or that the office


was created by the British North America Act, because if he takes that position his whole argument falls to the ground.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: I am contending that the right to appoint to the office of superior court judge is established under the British North America Act. What we are asking for is an amendment to the British North America Act to provide that judges cease to hold office on attaining the age of 75 years. The principles enunciated in the judgment to which I have referred are exactly applicable in this case. If the power to appoint to an office is established by statute, which is the British North America Act, and if that statute is amended in the proper constitutional method, to terminate the tenure of that office in a certain event, then any talk about breach of contract is just so much nonsense, so much fantasy, so much Alice in Wonderland, as was indulged in by the hon. member this afternoon.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: Page R. B. Bennett.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: Of course, I know the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) was a fervent follower of the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the minister, but it seems to me he is debating the amendment which has been disposed of by the house. He might proceed now to the main motion.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I could establish a case to the contrary but I will not do so, because I think it is important that we should get to the amendment which I propose to move with regard to the extension of time for the effective date of the coming into force of this legislation.
I had intended to refer to the question of whether or not this proposal should be founded upon an amendment to the British North America Act, and to refer my hon. friends to some statements by Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent, which I hope Your Honour will agree is a matter germane to the part of the discussion upon which I am now engaged.
There has been a question as to whether the main motion, which is the resolution before the house, should in fact be presented to the house by way of a constitutional amendment or whether it should have been referred to the Supreme Court of Canada for an opinion or whether, indeed, this parliament should not simply have assumed the right to amend the British North America Act instead of presenting an address to Her Majesty praying that the United Kingdom parliament should enact an amendment to the British North America Act. I think that what Mr. St. Laurent had to say in that regard is important, and I trust that whether or not the Supreme

Court of Canada and the privy council will be accepted as authorities by my hon. friends opposite, at least what was said by so eminent an authority as their recent leader and the recent prime minister of Canada will be accepted by them and might dispose of this argument.
In 1944, the Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent had this to say as reported on page 2248 of Hansard of that day:
Mr. Speaker, I think in about two minutes I can give the assurance that hon. members have sought, that at the very first opportunity the matter of an amendment to the British North America Act to deal with the provision which now gives judges of the provincial superior courts a life tenure in their office will be considered.
It was quite apparent that Mr. St. Laurent was prepared to introduce legislation or present to parliament a motion ending the so-called life tenure of superior court judges and to establish a retirement age. He went on to say this:
This is in my opinion a matter which should not be presented for amendment to the imperial parliament without previous discussion with the provinces, because the administration of justice and the establishment of the courts are matters that are within provincial jurisdiction.
It was obvious that Mr. St. Laurent felt that before you could bring in legislation which in effect provided for the elimination of an office in the courts or touched on the organization of the courts, that was a matter upon which you had to have the consent of the provinces and you had to submit the legislation to the United Kingdom parliament. This is exactly what we are doing here.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: Can the minister repeat the date of that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: It is 1944, page 2248.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: That was before the act of 1949.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
Before the act of 1949; yes, but if my friend is referring to the amendment to section 91 (1) of the British North America Act, let me direct my friend's attention to the important words of Mr. St. Laurent:
-the administration of justice and the establishment of the courts are matters that are within provincial jurisdiction.
Surely my hon. friend, who has made this passing, fantastic reference to section 91 (1) of the British North America Act, will not contend that this subject is within the purview of section 91 (1) when he himself pointed out today that that section enacted in 1949 applies only to matters that are not within provincial jurisdiction. Mr. St. Laurent continued:
It is my view that the proper procedure with respect to amendments to the British North America Act when dealing with any portion that gives
Amendment to B.N.A. Act jurisdiction to provincial legislatures should involve prior conference and consultation with the legislatures, and if it is sought to take away from them something which has been allotted to them, their consent should be obtained.
Then Mr. Bence interrupted':
That is not the case here, may I suggest.
Mr. St. Laurent replied:
I would consider that it is a case where there should be consultation with the provinces, because under section 92 they have jurisdiction in respect of the constitution of the courts, and section 99 is not placed specifically within dominion or provincial powers because it is something which affects both the powers of the governor in council and the powers of the provinces with regard to the setting up and the manning of the courts of justice. It is a matter which was on the agenda for discussion at the last provincial conference, and it certainly will be one of the matters to be considered at the next provincial conference.
As the house knows, unfortunately the government of that day was not able, nor was the following Liberal government able, to get any agreement whatever with the provinces with respect to this important matter. It was not until the year 1959, under the government of the present Prime Minister, that we were able to arrive at an agreement with the provinces with respect to this amendment. Now we find my hon. friends opposite indulging in the extraordinary tactics of suggesting that somehow or other, notwithstanding what their own former leader, an eminent prime minister and eminent jurist said, there is something improper, something vaguely doubtful about the method being followed by the present government in respect of the office of superior court judges. What we now see is quite the opposite from what I hoped and thought this afternoon would be the case, namely that my hon. friends opposite would recognize that, politics apart, here was a real step forward which could solve a constitutional dilemma of this country, on the contrary they appear to be so jealous and so activated by their jealousy they are prepared to attack what is being done on the flimsiest of grounds.
Mr. St. Laurent next discussed this subject in the House of Commons in 1946, as reported at page 2711 of Hansard, when he said, initially using a rhetorical question:
Is it still the opinion of the Minister of Justice that an amendment to the British North America Act, which would provide power to retire judges at a stated age, would require the consent of the provincial legislatures? To that my answer is that, notwithstanding the vote of last night, I persist in that view. I attempted to make it clear in that debate that I considered there had been an allocation of jurisdiction and that this parliament had no right to deal with matters which had been allocated to the provincial legislatures, and that when there was joint responsibility, if any change was to be made that would affect such

Amendment to B.N.A. Act
control as the provincial legislatures and governments have under the constitution, their consent would have to be obtained.
The present Prime Minister then asked:
Would it have to be the consent of all the provinces?
To this, Mr. St. Laurent replied:
In my opinion it would have to be the consent of all the provinces that would be affected thereby. I consider that they have been given jurisdiction sovereign powers, which they get not from this parliament but from the imperial parliament, and it is their jurisdiction; so we cannot take it from them without their consent, any more than if we wanted to take from a legislature of a state of the American union some of its powers.
Again, the present Prime Minister asked:
Every province would be in that position.
Mr. St. Laurent replied:
Every province would be in that position, my view.
It is in recognition of that position that the government has introduced this proposal in the form in which it is before the house, namely a resolution asking this house to adopt an address to Her Majesty praying that she will cause to be laid before the United Kingdom parliament an amendment to the British North America Act. This amendment covers not only the retirement age of judges of superior courts but, in order to make the matter clear beyond any doubt, it asks the United Kingdom parliament to provide, by way of an addition to the constitution of Canada, that the judges of district and county courts will also have their retirement age at 75 years confirmed. Inasmuch as the constitution of district and county courts is a matter of provincial jurisdiction and inasmuch as they are covered by section 92 (14) of the British North America Act I am at a loss to understand why my hon. friends take the extraordinary position that it is a retrograde step to ask that the matter be regularized by having it included in the constitution.
As I have pointed out it is the objective of the present Prime Minister-and it is one which we believe he will be successful in achieving in the same way as we have been successful in achieving this constitutional step forward, unlike our predecessors-it is his objective to reach a measure of agreement, which will result in the repatriation of the constitution so that the control of all the judges of Canada will be brought back to the parliament and to the legislatures of Canada instead of being left, as now, in the United Kingdom. On that basis we say that not only does this proposal not require any defence but that what is being done is right and proper and will place the position of district and county court judges on the basis on which they should be.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext: And on which they have never been.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
What would happen if they were not included in this address? One would have an extraordinary situation if he considers what would happen if they were left out. Section 1 would say that judges of superior courts shall hold office during good behaviour and shall be removable by the governor general on address of the Senate and House of Commons. Section 2 would say that judges of the superior, district and county courts shall cease to hold office on attaining the age of 75 years. This would be a most intolerable distinction and differentiation between the position of judges of district and county courts on the one hand and judges of superior courts on the other. Hence, on any basis on which you care to put it, Mr. Speaker, whether it be on the basis of rationalization of the position of judges of these courts or whether it be on the basis that we will not have any difference between judges of one court who are over 75 who may continue in office and judges who are appointed later but must retire at 75,- on whatever basis you put it-the proposal now before the house will bring a degree of rationality and a degree of order that is most desirable in establishing the position of the judges of our courts.
The only thing that remains then is to move the amendment on which I believe all parties in the house are agreed, namely that the effective date of the legislation to be adopted by the United Kingdom parliament be postponed to March 1, 1961. Accordingly, seconded by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), I move:
That the resolution be amended by deleting paragraph numbered "3" at the end thereof and substituting therefor the following:
3. This act shall come into force on the first day of March nineteen hundred and sixty one.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the amendment which the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) has just moved is, of course, necessary for the purposes which the government has in mind. However, I think I should point out that if this resolution had been proceeded with, as it should have been, much earlier than the present date, it would not have been necessary to provide for this amendment. In any event, the minister has not made clear that the amendment is really essential. However, there is nothing fundamental in the amendment itself, and one need not spend any time on it except to observe that once this resolution is passed the matter could be dealt with by the United Kingdom parliament, certainly before the

end of the date referred to in the third clause of the section of which this is an amendment.
This is an important matter, as both the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) have indicated. Any matter affecting the constitution of our country is a matter of great importance; and generally speaking, this debate has reflected our appreciation of the importance of the matter. Certainly any question affecting the judiciary of our country- whether it be the judges of the district and county courts or of the superior courts or, for that matter, anyone holding judicial office-is a matter of great importance.
It is true that in this common law jurisdiction we do not have the same mathematical appreciation of the division of the functions of government which Montesquieu thought applied to the form of government in Britain and perforce in Canada. But the fact is that the legislature and the executive share with the judicial arm the important function of preserving order in our free society. Any step taken that in any way violates or depreciates the integrity or the security of the judiciary in any of these levels is or should be a matter of concern.
Mr. Pallet!: Will the hon. member indicate the article from which he is quoting?

subtopic: ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
speechtext:
I was not quoting from any article. I was simply saying, for my hon. friend's benefit, that the great French writer Montesquieu referred to the British system of government as being made up of the executive, the legislature and the judiciary. I hope my hon. friend, who has had some training in political science, will remember who Montesquieu was.
The Prime Minister said that there was nothing unusual in what was being done today.
Of course, I do not know whether he had in mind that on previous occasions addresses had been presented to the United Kingdom parliament with regard to differing proposed constitutional amendments. I think that what we are now doing is unusual in that we are seeking to endow through this parliament which owes its existence constitutionally to a legislature outside of this country an authority to that legislature which that legislative body never claimed or never had. We are also seeking to ask this other authority, the parliament of the United Kingdom, to assume and to continue to assume a power which we might have removed from the United Kingdom parliament and placed forever within our own country.
Amendment to B.N.A. Act
For example, I would have liked to have seen this amendment provide, not that the United Kingdom should fix the ages of judges but that we should receive from the United Kingdom parliament the power ourselves to determine the circumstances of retirement of our superior court judges as to age or any other circumstance of tenure. But that is not what is being done in the resolution introduced by the Prime Minister.
Much of the argument has surrounded an alleged breach of contract. In so far as superior court judges are concerned what is now proposed by the government is that not only with regard to judges to be appointed but judges who are now serving on the bench they shall serve under conditions that did not attend when they were appointed. Because of that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate (Mr. Pickersgill) has argued that there is a breach of contract.
That in itself is an important matter. It is not the only point on which I would register complaint but it is a point of importance and one to which the Minister of Justice has addressed himself. He has said, of course, that to say there is a contract between the state and the judge under the circumstances outlined by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate is nonsense, and he cites as his authority the Reilly case. The Reilly case had nothing to do with a judicial appointment whatsoever. There may have been a breach of contract in that particular case-I am not saying that there was because I am not familiar with the details-but certainly that case does not in any way help us in the particular instance.
We do have parallel situations. Some of these were referred to today by the Leader of the Opposition. He referred to the amendment of 1927 and the arguments made on that occasion by Mr. Bennett, who complained along with Mr. Cahan-and there were not at that time, and perhaps not since, two better lawyers serving as members of this house- about the particular amendment on the ground, inter alia, that this was a breach of contract that the judges had been appointed under circumstances which they had a right to assume gave them an unlimited tenure of office, except for removal because of bad behaviour.
Mr. Bennett had dealt with this matter forcefully. When in 1933 the then solicitor general, Mr. Dupre, on March 4, moved the first reading of a bill to amend the Judges Act to provide that any judge continuing in office after 75 should suffer a reduction in salary of an amount equal to that which he would receive at 75, the leader of the opposition of that day, reminding the house of the

Amendment to B.N.A. Act position taken by the opposition in 1930 which had caused Mr. Lapointe, the minister of justice of that day, to alter the course which he had adopted, went on to remind the house that the provisions of the bill appeared to violate contracts between the crown and members of the judiciary.
In support of this position Mr. Lapointe the then minister of justice quoted Mr. Bennett as having said in 1927, under circumstances that are exactly the same as those which now confront the house:
What we are now doing involves a breach of the contract between the individual who holds office at the present time and the state, because his patent of office declares that he shall hold office during life or during good behaviour.
Then Mr. Bennett, in speaking of a particular judge, went on-

The point I was dealing with was that this very question had arisen and was dealt with by Mr. Bennett in terms similar to those used by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. I had not completed the sentence that Mr. Bennett had used when speaking of the case of a particular judge. He said:
That judge undoubtedly has a contract with the state which entitles him to receive a salary for life or until such time as he resigns. I think the government will be well advised to consider whether or not in all cases of this kind where the contract has been amended the judge should receive full salary. I think we must have regard to the terms and conditions under which the original contract was made. Although it may seem out of the ordinary that a judge should draw full salary when he is retired compulsorily, nevertheless good faith and morals in my judgment impose on us that obligation and it is an obligation we should not likely disregard.

So the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate was in good company. It must seem obvious that even though there might have been no written contract there are all the elements present in an implied contract when a judge is appointed to office. The argument of breach of contract is a strong argument, and one with which the Minister of Justice has not properly dealt.
I submit there is another argument, one which is even stronger, one that should impress the Minister of Justice. The judiciary must in every way be independent. Judges must be able by virtue of their tenure to carry out their functions in such a manner as not to be open in any way to interference except with regard to the matter of good behaviour, whether by parliament or by any body or authority in the country. This was what Sir Winston Churchill had in mind on April 23, 1954 when this kind of question was being discussed. That right hon. gentleman had this to say of the judges, and I think his words apply with equal force to the present situation:
There is nothing like them at all in our island. They are appointed for life. They cannot be dismissed by the executive government. They cannot be dismissed by the crown either by the prerogative or on the advice of ministers. They have to interpret the law according to their learning and conscience. They are distinguishable from the great officers of state and other servants of the executive, high or low, and from the leaders of commerce and industry. They are also clearly distinguishable from the holders of less exalted judicial office. Nothing but an address from both houses of parliament, assented to by the crown, can remove them.
With regard to those judges now on the bench, what is involved is this: we are interfering, by this measure, with their independence, an independence which is guaranteed to them under our system of law and under the governmental practice which prevails both here and in other commonwealth countries. That is what we are doing. It is not that we on this side of the house do not agree, in view of the acceptance in the public mind of a retiring age for judges, that the age of 75 is, perhaps the correct age. Our opposition does not arise because we are opposed to that principle. We are in favour of it, although we recognize that in our own country there have been judges away past the age of 75 who have rendered distinguished service in the prosecution of our system of law. Sir William Mulock, the late chief justice of the Supreme Court of Canada, Sir Lyman Duff, occur at once to my mind and we know the record in the United States of Mr. Justice Brandeis and Mr. Justice Holmes. We know the record of Lord Chief Justice Goddard in the United Kingdom, and other judicial luminaries who
Amendment to B.N.A. Act have contributed to the cause of justice notwithstanding their age. Nevertheless, we are in agreement with the government on the age of retirement. We ask simply that this should be applied in such a way as not to weaken the independence of the judiciary; that it should apply only to judges yet to be appointed, not to those who have already been appointed.
What is involved here is not only a breach of contract with regard to superior court judges but something more important. We are taking a step which I am sure any student or any serious lawyer would recognize as being a violation in principle of the necessary independence that must attach to the judiciary. Sir Winston Churchill felt so strongly on the subject that he went on in the same debate to say:
The principle of the complete independence of the judiciary from the executive is the foundation of many things in our island life. It has been widely imitated in varying degrees throughout the free world. It is perhaps one of the deepest gulfs between us and all forms of totalitarian rule. The only subordination which a judge knows in his judicial capacity is that which he owes to the existing body of legal doctrine enunciated in years past by his brethren on the bench, past and present, and upon the laws passed b.y parliament which have received the royal assent. The judge has not only to do justice between man and man. He also -and this is one of his most important functions, considered incomprehensible in some large parts of the world-has to do justice between the citizens and the state. The British judiciary, with its traditions and record, is one of the greatest living assets of our race and people and the independence of the judiciary is a part of our message to the ever-growing world which is rising so swifty around us.
Those words apply no less to the judiciary in this country. We should hesitate before taking any step which could be regarded in any way as a violation of the independence of the judiciary which we all postulate as an essential condition of our legal system.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext: And which is perfectly preserved in this legislation.

speechtext:
I do not believe that to be the case, if I may say so to the hon. member with respect, because we are saying to judges who have already been appointed for life: hereafter you will retire at the age of 75 years, notwithstanding the fact that when you were appointed no such limitation was part of the arrangement made by the government of the day. That certainly is an interference in theory at least, in principle, with the independence of those judges. One can conceive of situations-and I am not saying these presently exist, because I do not think the Prime Minister, who is a responsible lawyer, would concur-such as have happened in another country where the highest court was packed under conditions which caused

Amendment to B.N.A. Act the greatest controversy. Many learned societies and individuals in the United States were greatly concerned with the place of the judiciary in regard to the constitution as a result. That sort of thing could happen here. I am not saying that is the situation in the case before us. It is not, obviously. What I am saying is simply this: once a judge has been appointed for life we should not by an act of parliament take any step which they would not take in the United Kingdom parliament, as the words of Sir Winston Churchill so well establish.
With regard to the future, that is another matter. Judges if appointed in the future will know the circumstances and conditions of their appointment and if they are forced to retire at 75 no one could argue then that that compulsion or requirement in any way interfered with their tenure of office or with their independence. I am sure that the Prime Minister will agree that these words of Sir Winston Churchill have a cogency, a relevancy and an application to this situation in principle and it is the principle of the matter, of course, with which we are concerned.
The other matter on which we have differed from the administration is with regard to the position of district and county court judges. Those judges now hold their office under the Judges Act, Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, chapter 159, section 35. As both the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate and the Leader of the Opposition stated, this provision is one of long standing. It has been in practice ever since this confederation of ours came into being. The first act taken by this parliament to fix the age of judges of the district or county courts was in 1903. No one at that time contested that it was within the exclusive competence of this parliament, without any reference to the United Kingdom parliament, to limit the tenure of district judges. That question has never arisen. Notwithstanding that the administration of justice in this country has been under Liberal and Conservative administration, distinguished ministers of justice like Sir Charles Doherty, Mr. Lapointe, Mr. Guthrie, Mr. St. Laurent-

-have never questioned the right of this parliament to deal with the tenure of district court judges. To my knowledge the first suggestion ever made was in 1927 when a question was put to the then minister of justice by an hon. member of this house. The only other occasion to my knowledge when any doubt was raised about the situation is today through the resolution now before us. It will be remembered that in 1927 Mr. Boys, the then

hon. member for Simcoe, addressed a question to the then minister of justice, Mr. Lapointe, in this form:
While the minister is upon that point may I ask if there is any special provision in the British North America Act with respect to the retirement of county court judges? There was an amendment put through, if I remember correctly, in the year 1913 or the year 1914, providing for the compulsory retirement of county court judges upon reaching the age of 75 years. Is there any special provision in the British North America Act which provides for legislation of that character?
The minister said, "No". Mr. Cahan and Mr. Bennett were also active participants in the debate. They did not take exception to Mr. Lapointe's statement when he said:
No, not at all, but I would point out that section 99 applies only to the judges of the superior courts.
There was never any doubt about that. Apart from the question asked by Mr. Boys, the first doubt expressed was the suggestion we now have had from the Minister of Justice. What is the argument he adduces? The hon. gentleman tabled some correspondence with the attorneys general. I have read that correspondence and I am not aware that there is any letter in which real doubt is expressed as to the constitutional competence of the federal parliament to deal with the tenure of district judges. There is no suggestion in any of those letters that warrants the grave doubt which the Minister of Justice has sought to indicate exists in this matter by the attorneys general of the provinces.
If there were any doubt surely rather than take what might be regarded as a regressive step the Minister of Justice, before withdrawing from this parliament a power which we say undoubtedly exists should have sought an opinion from the Supreme Court of Canada as to whether or not this matter of the tenure of district judges was or was not a matter that came within the exclusive competence of the parliament of Canada.
We are asked by this resolution that the power which we have had for so many years, the power to deal with the tenure of office of district and county court judges, the duration of their function and their removal from office, be limited by the constitution, and by asking for the approval of the provinces the present government may well have made it necessary in future to consult the provinces if further changes become desirable.
The present government by this action will impose on the United Kingdom parliament additional power at a time when the effort of all of us is to bring to this country in the course of time, and we hope at the earliest possible time, full power to amend our own constitution. That is what our objective is. What the Minister of Justice

is now doing represents a regressive step. It will endow the United Kingdom parliament with a power which I am sure it does not want to exercise and which through the common endeavour of all of us in this house and I am sure of all provincial governments, we are anxious to see settled finally in this country once agreement can be obtained between the two senior levels of government.
Up until now this parliament has been free at any time to amend the constitution without reference to the provinces or to the British parliament in matters affecting the district and county court judges. The Prime Minister said that all of us in this house want to see reside in this country the power to amend our own constitution. The provinces now have that power in respect of matters that come under section 92 of the British North America Act. We have that power with regard to matters that come within our exclusive competence. But in respect of those matters that are of common concern to the federal government and the provinces the objective of most of us in this country, if agreement can be achieved on the part of the two senior levels of government, is to see that the power of constitutional amendment is given to the proper authority in this country.
What the minister is doing by this resolution is to reverse the process. If this resolution is passed, as undoubtedly it will be, it will extend to the parliament of the United Kingdom a power which since 1867 has resided outside the United Kingdom. Can anything be more unjustifiable in view of the fact that we all take pride in our sovereign status?
I ask the Minister of Justice to reconsider this particular phase of the resolution. I am sure that the point made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is valid. It is doubtful if we have any power to do what is proposed in the case of district court judges. It is certainly doubtful that the United Kingdom parliament will have any power to deal with this matter at all in so far as the tenure of district court judges is concerned. I should not be surprised if the United Kingdom parliament would refuse to deal with this particular phase of the resolution, as a matter outside its competence. If that should eventuate-and I am not so sure that it is not a pretty good anticipation- then we would be faced in this country with a most ridiculous situation.
By incorporating an express provision of the British North America Act in this resolution the government is now putting itself in the position of making it necessary hereafter to consult the provinces if at any time

I am not saying whether or not it is a good thing that there was no consultation in this matter, but what I am saying is that it is our duty in this house to follow the constitution. The constitution of Canada, the British North America Act, by its clear, implicit terms does not impose any obligation on this parliament, or on the executive of this parliament, to consult the provinces with regard to the tenure of district court judges.
The situation with regard to superior court judges is different. Mr. St. Laurent took the position that with regard to superior court judges it was a matter of common concern to the federal and the provincial governments. It is not a question of what my hon. friend would like to see. The question is, what is the law? The law is clear in this regard. Section 96 of the British North America Act provides that the governor general shall appoint the judges of the superior district and county courts in each province except those of the courts of probate in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. The act makes no provision whatsoever as to the tenure of offices of judges of the district and county courts; but section 99 does provide that-and it is worth while to read it:
The fudges of the superior courts shall hold office during good behaviour, but shall be removable by the Governor General on address of the Senate and House of Commons.
Therefore it is not very difficult to see it is obvious that if the British North America Act provided only with respect to judges of the superior courts that they could hold office during good behaviour, that is to say for life, it must follow that no such condition attached to the appointment of district and county court judges, and that those who appointed them would be free to make the appointments for a lesser time than life. That has been the practice for 90 years of Liberal and Conservative administrations. That principle was practised in the days of Mr. Bennett, in the days of Sir Robert Borden, in the days of Mr. Meighen, in the days of Sir Charles Tupper, in the days of Sir John A. Macdonald, and now it is going to be changed by the Hon. Davie Fulton. Surely, that is the answer to my hon. friend.

speechtext:
Text of Letter on disarmament dated June 2,
1960 from the Chairman of the Council of Ministers of the U.S.S.R. to the Prime Minister of Canada.
His Excellency Mr. John G. Diefenbaker, Prime Minister of Canada,
City of Ottawa.
Dear Mr. Prime Minister:
I would like to address you on the question of general and complete disarmament, which is the most important question confronting the world at the present time. Nowadays, in the age of atom, space rockets and electronics, the necessity to take daring and far-reaching actions aimed at finding a solution of the disarmament problem has become especially acute. Is it not obvious that now common sense cannot be reconciled any longer with the whirl of armaments, which is pulling toward an unprecedented disaster and which is indeed perniciously affecting all aspects of the life of society?
In the course of its preparations for the Paris conference of the heads of government, the Soviet government has worked out proposals which constitute the elaboration of the general and complete disarmament program which I, on behalf of the Soviet government submitted to the fourteenth session of the U.N. general assembly last September.
In those proposals we took into consideration certain observations expressed by our partners in negotiations and, in particular, the ideas expressed by the government of France to the effect that at the beginning of the implementation of the disarmament program measures should be undertaken to eliminate the means of delivering nuclear weapons to targets. Some other proposals put forward by a number of governments, including those made in the course of discussions in the ten-nation committee on disarmament, have also been taken into consideration. However, we were unfortunately unable to discuss those proposals at the meeting of the heads of government.
Latest developments have not reduced but on the contrary increased the determination of the Soviet government to seek a radical solution of the disarmament problem, the liquidation of the armaments race, which is dangerous and useless for the peoples. The Soviet government, being guided by its invariable policy of peaceful co-existence among
states, intends, as it has before, to do everything necessary for the invigoration of the international situation and the improvement of relations among states.
Upon my return from Paris to Moscow the Soviet government discussed the situation obtained and came to the conclusion that it was necessary to submit the proposals on general and complete disarmament which had been prepared for the conference of the heads of government for the consideration by the governments of all states.
A relevant document containing the proposals of the Soviet government on the implementation of general and complete disarmament is transmitted to you together with this message.
We are convinced that these proposals meet the requirements set forth in the resolution on general and complete disarmament unanimously adopted by the U.N. general assembly on November 20, 1959.
I would like to draw your attention to the fact that the program of the Soviet government envisages already at the first stage prohibition and destruction of all means of delivering nuclear weapon missiles of all ranges, military aircraft, surface naval vessels which can be used as carriers of nuclear weapons, submarines of all classes and types, all artillery systems, as well as other means which can be used as carriers of atomic and hydrogen weapons.
Obviously, the security of states can be duly safeguarded if only all means, without exception, of delivering atomic and hydrogen weapons are eliminated from the armaments of states and are destroyed. It goes without saying that a simultaneous elimination of all military bases on foreign territories and withdrawal of foreign troops therefrom is necessary, since the retention of such bases and troops could be used for aggression against nearby states.
The implementation of these measures at the very beginning of the disarmament program would remove the danger of a surprise nuclear war being unleashed and would change radically the international situation.
At subsequent stages measures for the prohibition of nuclear and other weapons of mass destruction, for the elimination of armies and war machinery of states would be put into practice, thus making it possible to preclude

speakerposition: stagedirection

With the gradual implementation of the disarmament program a part of the funds thus released should be used to render economic assistance to the underdeveloped countries.
You will see from our proposals that they contain detailed provisions for control over disarmament measures which would not allow anyone to evade the observance of the agreement on general and complete disarmament. We have worked out specific measures on control according to respective stages of the disarmament program, we have indicated objects for control, defined the structure and composition of the control body, the rights and powers of on the spot inspectors. Our new proposals containing detailed provisions for the control constitute still another proof of the Soviet union being in favour of a strict and effective control over disarmament.
The Soviet government believes that these proposals should be given a comprehensive study first of all in the ten-nation committee on disarmament which is to resume its work in Geneva in a few days.
I would also like to emphasize that the Soviet government entertains serious doubts that the western powers represented on this body really want disarmament. Although these powers did vote in the general assembly for the resolution on general and complete disarmament, the impression is that, in fact, they are not prepared to implement it.
As is known, the western powers came out in the committee with such a plan which, given all the desire, cannot be called a plan of general and complete disarmament. Even after the implementation of that plan there would remain armies, military aircraft, tanks, guns, military bases in foreign territories, general staffs and nuclear bombs. As a matter of fact, the western powers propose control without disarmament. Frankly speaking, such control is nothing else but intelligence and espionage.
No government attentive to the sovereign rights of states can accept this.
The Soviet union desires actual and complete disarmament, destruction of all types of weapons and establishment of a strict control over disarmament so that no one would be able to arm and no one would be able to threaten with war.
May I express, Mr. Prime Minister, the hope that the proposals of the Soviet government, prompted solely by the desire to facilitate and expedite the conclusion of an argeement on this most important question of our time, the
question of general and complete disarmament, will meet with understanding and support of your government.
Respectfully,
N. Khrushchev.
The Basic Provisions of a Treaty on General and Complete Disarmament
On the 18th of September 1959 the Soviet government put forward for consideration by the United Nations a proposal for general and complete disarmament. It submitted that proposal, proceeding from a firm conviction that the complete disarmament of all states, elimination of all means of war constitute the most efficient and-under the existing conditions-the most practicable way to prevent the outbreak of a rocket and nuclear war, so disastrous for nations; and to ensure a lasting peace on earth.
The balance of power obtained at present in the world when an aggressor is not able to unleash war against peace-loving states with impunity; the destructive power, without parallel in the history of mankind, of the modern weapons, which are able to effect a quick annihilation of whole states; the feasibility of almost instantaneous delivery of such weapons to any point on the globe- all these factors make war as a means of solving international arguments an obvious folly. The peaceful coexistence of states with different social systems, which the Soviet union, as well as other socialist countries, has always been championing, is a real fact. Peaceful coexistence, however, cannot be durable enough, peace cannot be considered to be reliably secured as long as the arms race is being continued, as long as states have at their disposal the means to attack other countries with lightning speed and possess gigantic stockpiles of weapons, nuclear weapons included.
Nowadays truly fantastic sums of money are being spent on armaments. Suffice it to say, that certain types of modern bombers cost more than their weight in gold. And is it not a fact that many types of armaments become obsolete even before they are shipped from the factories and are scrapped? The arms race becomes a senseless waste of human labour and of material. Sums at present spent by states to produce and stockpile weapons would alone suffice to put an end to starvation on the whole of the globe.
The fact that the energy of hundreds of millions of people and the values they create are spent on the preparation for war, whose inadmissibility becomes clearer with every day, cannot be tolerated any longer. The mankind of today with its wonderful achievements in conquering nature and developing spiritual values deserves a better fate.

At present the great goal, the dream of many generations-to put an end to wars, to preclude war from the life of human society altogether-have become practicable, possible to achieve. This goal can be achieved by means of destroying all types of weapons and disbanding all armies of the world, that is by general and complete disarmament. This is the only genuinely reliable basis, on which under the present conditions a lasting, unbreakable peace among all states can rest.
General and complete disarmament cannot give advantages to any party. This makes it possible to remove many of the obstacles which arose whenever it was only partial disarmament measures that were dealt with and when some states feared that the implementation of such measures might upset the balance of forces and prove detrimental to their security. The conclusion of an agreement on general and complete disarmament would also make it much easier to exercise international control over the disarmament measures for, if complete disarmament is arrived at, states will have no reasons to conceal anything from one another and it will be possible to exercise complete control.
The proposal of the Soviet union on general and complete disarmament met with enthusiastic approval in all the countries of the world. It added new strength to the aspirations of peoples to rid forever of the nightmarish threat of a rocket and nuclear war. No government opposed that proposal. The United Nations unanimously endorsed the idea of general and complete disarmament and confirmed that the question of such disarmament is the most important one facing the world today. The appeal of the U.N. general assembly to the governments to do their utmost to reach a constructive solution of this problem as soon as possible puts great moral obligation upon all states.
To implement that appeal of the United Nations and to make come true the hopes of people who call for disarmament, it is necessary that the governments on whom rests the main responsibility for reaching an international agreement on this question take concrete steps toward the preparation and conclusion of such an agreement without any further delay.
The Soviet government makes all efforts to achieve as soon as possible practical results in the disarmament talks-to work out and sign an agreement on general and complete disarmament.
As is known, the Soviet union's proposals of September 18, 1959, contain a concrete program for carrying out general and complete disarmament by three stages within the time limit of four years. It was proposed to effect at the first stage under international
control a substantial reduction of conventional armed forces and armaments of states, at the second-to complete the elimination of the remaining contingents of these armed forces and to eliminate military bases on foreign territories and at the third-to destroy all types of nuclear and rocket weapons and to carry out other measures concluding general and complete disarmament.
When proposing this sequence of disarmament measures the Soviet union took into account the views of the western powers who referring at previous disarmament negotiations to the superiority of the U.S.S.R. in the armed forces and conventional armaments, spoke out for the measures in the field of nuclear disarmament to be put off to the last stage. As regards the Soviet government it has always been in favour of making a war with the use of weapons of mass destruction impossible and it considers the sooner it is carried out, the better.
During the meetings and talks among leading statesmen that have taken place in recent months, as well as in the course of the work of the 10-nation committee on disarmament which was entrusted with the elaboration of measures for the realisation of the decision of the U.N. general assembly on general and complete disarmament, the views and proposals of sides on the questions concerning disarmament have been set forth in detai1 and specified.
The Soviet government invariably upholding its proposal for general and complete disarmament as one consistent with the great goal of ensuring a durable peace on earth, in which all nations barring none are interested in, at the same time is prepared to take into consideration any constructive observations and wishes of other participants of the negotiations, that are conducive to the achievement of an agreement on the practical realisation of disarmament.
In the course of the negotiations an opinion was expressed by some powers, particularly by France, that disarmament should be started with the prohibition and destruction of the means of delivering to target nuclear, chemical and biological weapons such as war missiles, air force, naval vessels and so on, and at the same time the necessity for the simultaneous elimination by states of their military bases on foreign territories was taken into account.
The government of the U.S.S.R. is still of opinion that the order of carrying out disarmament measures stipulated in its proposal of September 18, 1959, is fully consistent with the goal of the practical realisation of general and complete disarmament. Nevertheless, trying to facilitate in every possible way an early
